papers.conclusion: The analysis offers a new lens for advancing cross-lingual interactions and better leveraging models' internalized multilingual knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
X Transplant has mutually beneficial effects on multilingual capability and cultural adaptability, especially for low-resource languages and cultures.
Attention modules play a pivotal role in supporting multilingual understanding, while feed-forward modules are more adept at capturing culture-specific knowledge.
The upper-bound performance of X Transplant reveals a significant underutilization of current LLMs' multilingual potential.
English boosts multilingual capability, while non-English improves cultural adaptability.
papers.abstract: Current large language models (LLMs) often exhibit imbalances in multilingual capabilities and cultural adaptability, largely attributed to their English-centric pre-training data. In this paper, we introduce and investigate a cross-lingual latent transplantation (XTransplant) framework, which aims to further exploit the model's internalized multilingual knowledge during inference and examine its effects on the multilingual capability and cultural adaptability of LLMs. XTransplant framework enables models to harness the complementary strengths of both English and non-English resources by transplanting latent activations across languages. Through extensive analysis, we empirically demonstrate that XTransplant, a form of cross-lingual interaction, has mutually beneficial effects on the multilingual capability and cultural adaptability of LLMs, particularly for low-resource languages and cultures. We further reveal that attention modules play a pivotal role in supporting multilingual understanding, while feed-forward modules are more adept at capturing culture-specific knowledge. In addition, we conduct in-depth analysis of XTransplant's stability, effectiveness, and generalizability. By probing the upper bound performance of XTransplant, we expose the considerable underutilization of current LLMs' multilingual potential-a challenge that remains open. We hope our analysis offers a new lens for advancing cross-lingual interactions and better leveraging models' internalized multilingual knowledge.

papers.title: Unveiling Multilinguality in Transformer Models: Exploring Language Specificity in Feed-Forward Networks
papers.research_question: Do neurons in the feed-forward networks of multilingual transformer models exhibit language-specific or language-agnostic behavior across layers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that in multilingual transformer models, feed-forward network layers near the input and output are more language-specific, whereas middle layers are more language-agnostic.
papers.conclusion: The study reveals that language specificity in FFNs is higher near the input and output layers, and training data imbalance influences detector activations.
papers.key_findings:
Layers closest to the input and output exhibit more language-specific behavior compared to middle layers.
The number of detectors triggered by English prefixes is higher than for Czech, reflecting training data imbalance.
The number of unique detectors varies across layers, with sparsity patterns observed in FFN activations.
Linear classifiers can predict the language of input prefixes from detector activations with higher accuracy in input and output layers.
Czech-specific detectors decrease in middle layers, suggesting semantic processing uses more language-agnostic detectors.
papers.limitation:
Analysis is limited to only the XGLM model.
Study is centred on the Czech-English language pair, and findings may not generalize to other languages.
Lack of qualitative analysis of linguistic cues triggering detector activation.
future_direction: Extend analysis to more language pairs and other multilingual autoregressive language models.
papers.abstract: Recent research suggests that the feed-forward module within Transformers can be viewed as a collection of key-value memories, where the keys learn to capture specific patterns from the input based on the training examples. The values then combine the output from the 'memories' of the keys to generate predictions about the next token. This leads to an incremental process of prediction that gradually converges towards the final token choice near the output layers. This interesting perspective raises questions about how multilingual models might leverage this mechanism. Specifically, for autoregressive models trained on two or more languages, do all neurons (across layers) respond equally to all languages? No! Our hypothesis centers around the notion that during pretraining, certain model parameters learn strong language-specific features, while others learn more language-agnostic (shared across languages) features. To validate this, we conduct experiments utilizing parallel corpora of two languages that the model was initially pretrained on. Our findings reveal that the layers closest to the network's input or output tend to exhibit more language-specific behaviour compared to the layers in the middle.

papers.title: Can you map it to English? The Role of Cross-Lingual Alignment in Multilingual Performance of LLMs
papers.research_question: How does an LLM's ability to align representations of non-English inputs to English impact its performance on NLU tasks, and does misalignment causally explain failures?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that cross-lingual alignment with English in middle layers is associated with and causally affects LLM performance on multilingual NLU tasks.
papers.conclusion: Cross-lingual semantic alignment in localized middle layers contributes causally to non-English correctness in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Transfer Success (TS) instances exhibit higher cross-lingual alignment with English than Transfer Failure (TF) instances.
Activation patching of English activations into non-English forward passes can correct incorrect predictions, indicating causal role of alignment.
Middle layers (e.g., layers 16-25) are critical for alignment and effective patching.
Control patching experiments show that semantic alignment, not just target token bias, drives corrections in specific middle layers.
Alignment peaks in middle layers and varies by language typology, with closer languages to English showing higher alignment.
papers.limitation:
Scope restricted to discriminative NLU tasks.
Benchmarks may have translation artifacts due to human translation from English.
Only analyzes bilingual alignment with English, not between other languages.
future_direction: Exploring targeted steering at inference time to leverage English activations for enhancing performance on non-English languages.
Studying potential downsides such as inflated confidence and erasure of valuable local, non-English knowledge.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can answer prompts in many languages, despite being trained predominantly on English; yet, the mechanisms driving this generalization remain poorly understood. This work asks: How does an LLM's ability to align representations of non-English inputs to English impact its performance on natural language understanding (NLU) tasks? We study the role of representation alignment in instance-level task decisions, complementing prior analyses conducted both at the language level and task-independently. We introduce the Discriminative Alignment Index ($\DALI$) to quantify instance-level alignment across 24 languages other than English and three distinct NLU tasks. Results show that incorrect NLU predictions are strongly associated with lower representation alignment with English in the model's middle layers. Through activation patching, we show that incorrect predictions in languages other than English can be fixed by patching their parallel English activations in the middle layers, thereby demonstrating the causal role of representation (mis)alignment in cross-lingual correctness.

papers.title: SVCCA: Singular Vector Canonical Correlation Analysis for Deep Learning\n Dynamics and Interpretability
papers.research_question: What is the intrinsic dimensionality of neural network layers and how do learning dynamics progress during training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SVCCA, a method for comparing neural network representations that is invariant to affine transforms, and uses it to show that layers have lower intrinsic dimensionality than the number of neurons, and that networks converge from the bottom up during training.
papers.conclusion: SVCCA is a powerful method for comparing neural network representations, providing insights into learning dynamics, intrinsic dimensionality, and enabling applications like model compression and improved training regimes.
papers.key_findings:
The intrinsic dimensionality of a layer is less than the number of neurons, and projecting onto the top SVCCA directions preserves accuracy without retraining.
Networks converge from the bottom up during training, with lower layers solidifying their representations earlier than higher layers.
SVCCA captures semantic class information, with similar classes having similar sensitivities in the network.
Freeze Training, based on the bottom-up convergence, can save computation and improve generalization by sequentially freezing lower layers during training.
SVCCA can be used for model compression by projecting layer outputs onto top SVCCA directions, reducing parameter count and computational cost.
papers.abstract:
We propose a new technique, Singular Vector Canonical Correlation Analysis
(SVCCA), a tool for quickly comparing two representations in a way that is both
invariant to affine transform (allowing comparison between different layers and
networks) and fast to compute (allowing more comparisons to be calculated than
with previous methods). We deploy this tool to measure the intrinsic
dimensionality of layers, showing in some cases needless over-parameterization;
to probe learning dynamics throughout training, finding that networks converge
to final representations from the bottom up; to show where class-specific
information in networks is formed; and to suggest new training regimes that
simultaneously save computation and overfit less. Code:
https://github.com/google/svcca/

papers.title: On the Sub-layer Functionalities of Transformer Decoder
papers.research_question: How do source and target information evolve within the Transformer decoder layer-by-layer and module-by-module? How does the Source Exploitation Module (SEM) exploit source information in different layers? How does the Information Fusion Module (IFM) fuse source and target information?
papers.core_contribution: This paper analyzes the functionalities of sub-layers within the Transformer decoder for neural machine translation, introducing a universal probing scheme. A key finding is that the residual feed-forward module can be removed with minimal performance loss, significantly boosting speed.
papers.conclusion: The analysis provides insights into how the Transformer decoder leverages source and target information across layers and modules. These findings can inspire architectural improvements, such as incorporating external alignment signals, exploring different sub-layer stacking orders, and pruning redundant components for efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
The Source Exploitation Module (SEM) guides the representation evolution of both source and target information within the decoder.
Higher-layer SEMs focus on word alignment, while lower-layer SEMs gather broader source context.
The Target Exploitation Module (TEM) is critical for building word alignments in SEM, but its stacking order with SEM is not essential.
The Information Fusion Module (IFM) can be simplified to a single Add&Norm operation, removing the feed-forward network, with minimal translation quality loss and significant speed improvements.
The simplified decoder (without feed-forward modules) achieves comparable BLEU scores while increasing training and inference speed by 11-14% for Base models and up to 50% for inference on some tasks.
future_direction: Improving word alignment of higher SEMs by incorporating external alignment signals.
Exploring the stacking order of SEM, TEM and IFM sub-layers for more effective information transformation.
Applying the analysis methods to other sequence-to-sequence tasks like summarization and grammar error correction.
Exploring other architectures such as RNMT, ConvS2S, or document-level NMT.
papers.abstract: There have been significant efforts to interpret the encoder of Transformer-based encoderdecoder architectures for neural machine translation (NMT); meanwhile, the decoder remains largely unexamined despite its critical role. During translation, the decoder must predict output tokens by considering both the source-language text from the encoder and the target-language prefix produced in previous steps. In this work, we study how Transformerbased decoders leverage information from the source and target languages -developing a universal probe task to assess how information is propagated through each module of each decoder layer. We perform extensive experiments on three major translation datasets (WMT En-De, En-Fr, and En-Zh). Our analysis provides insight on when and where decoders leverage different sources. Based on these insights, we demonstrate that the residual feed-forward module in each Transformer decoder layer can be dropped with minimal loss of performance -a significant reduction in computation and number of parameters, and consequently a significant boost to both training and inference speed.

papers.title: Neuron-Level Analysis of Cultural Understanding in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the existence and distribution of culture-general and culture-specific neurons in LLMs? How do these neurons contribute to cultural understanding and what are their potential engineering applications?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces CULNIG, a gradient-based method to identify culture-general and culture-specific neurons in LLMs. It finds that these neurons are few (<1% of all neurons) and concentrated in shallow to middle MLP layers, and that suppressing them significantly degrades cultural understanding while minimally affecting general NLU tasks.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that culture-general and culture-specific neurons exist in LLMs and play a crucial role in cultural understanding. The findings provide insights into the internal mechanisms of LLMs and offer practical guidance for model training and engineering.
papers.key_findings:
Culture-general and culture-specific neurons account for less than 1% of all neurons and are concentrated in shallow to middle MLP layers.
Suppressing culture-general neurons substantially degrades performance on cultural benchmarks (by up to 30%) while performance on general NLU benchmarks remains largely unaffected.
Culture-specific neurons support knowledge of not only the target culture but also related cultures.
Training on NLU benchmarks can diminish models' cultural understanding when updating modules containing many culture-general neurons.
The gradient-based attribution method (CULNIG) effectively identifies neurons that contribute to cultural understanding.
future_direction: Further investigation of the discrepancy between CULNIG and CAPE neuron distributions
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed worldwide, ensuring their fair and comprehensive cultural understanding is important. However, LLMs exhibit cultural bias and limited awareness of underrepresented cultures, while the mechanisms underlying their cultural understanding remain underexplored. To fill this gap, we conduct a neuron-level analysis to identify neurons that drive cultural behavior, introducing a gradient-based scoring method with additional filtering for precise refinement. We identify both culture-general neurons contributing to cultural understanding regardless of cultures, and culture-specific neurons tied to an individual culture. These neurons account for less than 1% of all neurons and are concentrated in shallow to middle MLP layers. We validate their role by showing that suppressing them substantially degrades performance on cultural benchmarks (by up to 30%), while performance on general natural language understanding (NLU) benchmarks remains largely unaffected. Moreover, we show that culture-specific neurons support knowledge of not only the target culture, but also related cultures. Finally, we demonstrate that training on NLU benchmarks can diminish models' cultural understanding when we update modules containing many culture-general neurons. These findings provide insights into the internal mechanisms of LLMs and offer practical guidance for model training and engineering. Our code is available at https://github.com/ynklab/CULNIG

papers.title: Dissecting Catastrophic Forgetting in Continual Learning by Deep Visualization
papers.research_question: How does catastrophic forgetting occur in deep neural networks during continual learning, and which components are most affected?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Auto DeepVis, a tool to automatically identify which components in a neural network are most affected by catastrophic forgetting during continual learning, and introduces critical freezing, a method to mitigate forgetting by freezing these plastic components.
papers.conclusion: Auto DeepVis effectively identifies forgetting layers in neural networks, and critical freezing based on these findings helps mitigate catastrophic forgetting, serving as a supplementary tool for continual learning.
papers.key_findings:
Auto DeepVis identifies convolutional blocks 3 and 4 in ResNet-50 as the most plastic layers prone to catastrophic forgetting.
Critical freezing, which freezes these plastic layers, improves performance on both past and new tasks compared to fine-tuning and other freezing baselines.
The forgetting effect is quantified using IoU between feature maps, showing a decrease in similarity as new tasks are learned.
In the decoder, the LSTM layer is crucial for caption generation, while the linear layer can be updated with less impact on forgetting.
The approach provides a complementary strategy to existing continual learning methods by using interpretability to guide mitigation.
papers.limitation:
The tool only considers the filter with the highest IoU, which is a crude assumption and may not capture all forgetting effects.
The method has not been validated on tasks beyond image captioning, limiting its generalizability.
RNN components are not fully visualized or understood, requiring further interpretability methods.
future_direction: Develop a more automated and refined version of Auto DeepVis.
Extend the analysis to consider multiple filters per convolutional block.
Scale the method to other tasks beyond image captioning.
papers.abstract: Interpreting the behaviors of Deep Neural Networks (usually considered as a black box) is critical especially when they are now being widely adopted over diverse aspects of human life. Taking the advancements from Explainable Artificial Intelligent, this paper proposes a novel technique called Auto DeepVis to dissect catastrophic forgetting in continual learning. A new method to deal with catastrophic forgetting named critical freezing is also introduced upon investigating the dilemma by Auto DeepVis. Experiments on a captioning model meticulously present how catastrophic forgetting happens, particularly showing which components are forgetting or changing. The effectiveness of our technique is then assessed; and more precisely, critical freezing claims the best performance on both previous and coming tasks over baselines, proving the capability of the investigation. Our techniques could not only be supplementary to existing solutions for completely eradicating catastrophic forgetting for life-long learning but also explainable.

papers.title: Simulated Adoption: Decoupling Magnitude and Direction in LLM In-Context Conflict Resolution
papers.research_question: Does the suppression of parametric knowledge in the residual stream arise from the radial dilution of the signal's magnitude, or from an angular displacement induced by orthogonal interference?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs resolve in-context knowledge conflicts through orthogonal interference in the residual stream, rotating hidden states rather than diluting signal magnitude, challenging scalar confidence metrics.
papers.conclusion: LLMs resolve knowledge conflicts via orthogonal interference in the residual stream, simulating adoption without erasing internal knowledge, highlighting the need for vectorial monitoring over scalar metrics.
papers.key_findings:
Logit decay for correct tokens occurs under conflicting contexts, most pronounced in final layers.
Norm dynamics vary by architecture; Llama-3.1-8B shows dilution, but Qwen-3-4B and GLM-4-9B maintain stable norms.
Interference vectors are quasi-orthogonal to truth directions, supporting the orthogonal interference hypothesis.
Angular deviation correlates strongly with performance drop, indicating geometric rotation is the dominant mechanism.
Compliance is characterized by simulated adoption, where internal truth is bypassed, not erased.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on the Linear Representation Hypothesis, assuming truth and context interact as linear vectors.
Dataset scope restricted to fact-based QA tasks (MMLU), may not generalize to other tasks.
Focus on final residual state before unembedding, not layer-wise evolution of interference vectors.
Sample size of three architectures may not capture behaviors of larger or MoE models.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) frequently prioritize conflicting in-context information over pre-existing parametric memory, a phenomenon often termed sycophancy or compliance. However, the mechanistic realization of this behavior remains obscure, specifically how the model resolves these knowledge conflicts through compliance, and whether this suppression arises from signal magnitude dilution or directional geometric alteration within the residual stream. To resolve this, we conducted a layer-wise geometric analysis across Qwen-3-4B, Llama-3.1-8B, and GLM-4-9B, decomposing the residual stream updates induced by counter-factual contexts into radial (norm-based) and angular (cosine-based) components. Our empirical results reject the universality of the "Manifold Dilution" hypothesis, as two of the three architectures maintained stable residual norms despite exhibiting significant performance degradation on factual queries. Instead, we observed that compliance is consistently characterized by "Orthogonal Interference," where the conflicting context injects a steering vector that is quasi-orthogonal to the ground-truth direction, effectively rotating the hidden state representation. This suggests that models do not "unlearn" or suppress the magnitude of internal truths but rather employ a mechanism of geometric displacement to bypass the correct unembedding vector, effectively simulating adoption while preserving the original structural magnitude. These findings challenge scalar confidence metrics for detecting hallucinations and underscore the necessity of vectorial monitoring to distinguish between genuine knowledge integration and superficial in-context mimicry.

papers.title: Discovering Salient Neurons in Deep NLP Models
papers.research_question: Can we identify subsets of neurons that learn specific linguistic properties, and how is linguistic knowledge localized, distributed, and affected by fine-tuning in NLP models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Linguistic Correlation Analysis (LCA) for extracting salient neurons in NLP models, revealing that linguistic knowledge is localized in lower layers for basic properties and distributed in higher layers for complex concepts, with variations across models and during fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: The LCA method provides insights into how linguistic knowledge is encoded in neurons, showing localization patterns and redistribution during fine-tuning, with implications for model understanding and transfer learning.
papers.key_findings:
Small subsets of neurons can predict different linguistic tasks.
Neurons for basic lexical information are localized in lower layers, while those for complex concepts are in higher layers.
Linguistic information is redundantly preserved across neurons.
During transfer learning, salient linguistic neurons relocate to lower layers in some models like RoBERTa and XLNet.
Multilingual models exhibit similar neuron distribution for concepts across different languages.
future_direction: Pinpointing specific concepts regressed to lower layers versus those retained in higher layers during fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: While a lot of work has been done in understanding representations learned within deep NLP models and what knowledge they capture, little attention has been paid towards individual neurons. We present a technique called as Linguistic Correlation Analysis to extract salient neurons in the model, with respect to any extrinsic property - with the goal of understanding how such a knowledge is preserved within neurons. We carry out a fine-grained analysis to answer the following questions: (i) can we identify subsets of neurons in the network that capture specific linguistic properties? (ii) how localized or distributed neurons are across the network? iii) how redundantly is the information preserved? iv) how fine-tuning pre-trained models towards downstream NLP tasks, impacts the learned linguistic knowledge? iv) how do architectures vary in learning different linguistic properties? Our data-driven, quantitative analysis illuminates interesting findings: (i) we found small subsets of neurons that can predict different linguistic tasks, ii) with neurons capturing basic lexical information (such as suffixation) localized in lower most layers, iii) while those learning complex concepts (such as syntactic role) predominantly in middle and higher layers, iii) that salient linguistic neurons are relocated from higher to lower layers during transfer learning, as the network preserve the higher layers for task specific information, iv) we found interesting differences across pre-trained models, with respect to how linguistic information is preserved within, and v) we found that concept exhibit similar neuron distribution across different languages in the multilingual transformer models. Our code is publicly available as part of the NeuroX toolkit.

papers.title: Fortuitous Forgetting in Connectionist Networks
papers.research_question: Can forgetting be beneficial for learning in artificial neural networks? The paper introduces the forget-and-relearn paradigm to study this.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the forget-and-relearn framework, which unifies iterative training algorithms and shows that selective forgetting of undesirable information leads to improved generalization. It demonstrates this by designing targeted forgetting operations that outperform existing methods.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that forget-and-relearn is a powerful framework for understanding iterative training, where selective forgetting of undesirable information and relearning of consistent features leads to improved generalization and compositionality.
papers.key_findings:
Weight perturbation (reinitialization or zeroing) disproportionately affects undesirable information such as difficult examples and non-compositional language mappings.
Later Layer Forgetting (LLF), which reinitializes later layers, significantly improves generalization performance on image classification tasks compared to existing iterative methods.
Partial Balanced Forgetting (PBF), which reinitializes weights in both sender and receiver, improves the compositionality of emergent languages in the Lewis game.
The forget-and-relearn framework provides a unifying perspective for iterative training algorithms, explaining their success through selective forgetting.
The relearning stage reinforces features that are consistently useful under different initial conditions induced by forgetting.
papers.limitation: There is a Goldilocks zone of forgetting: too little forgetting leads to retraining to the same basin, while too much forgetting prevents accumulation of progress.
future_direction: Exploring the Goldilocks zone of forgetting to understand optimal forgetting amounts.
Developing algorithms that capture the benefits of forget-and-relearn without iterative training.
papers.abstract: Forgetting is often seen as an unwanted characteristic in both human and machine learning. However, we propose that forgetting can in fact be favorable to learning. We introduce "forget-and-relearn" as a powerful paradigm for shaping the learning trajectories of artificial neural networks. In this process, the forgetting step selectively removes undesirable information from the model, and the relearning step reinforces features that are consistently useful under different conditions. The forget-and-relearn framework unifies many existing iterative training algorithms in the image classification and language emergence literature, and allows us to understand the success of these algorithms in terms of the disproportionate forgetting of undesirable information. We leverage this understanding to improve upon existing algorithms by designing more targeted forgetting operations. Insights from our analysis provide a coherent view on the dynamics of iterative training in neural networks and offer a clear path towards performance improvements.

papers.title: The Rise and Down of Babel Tower: Investigating the Evolution Process of Multilingual Code Large Language Model
papers.research_question: How do the multilingual capabilities of LLMs evolve during the pre-training process?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the Babel Tower Hypothesis to explain how LLMs evolve multilingual capabilities during pre-training, and introduces a method to optimize pre-training data distribution for multilingual code LLMs.
papers.conclusion: The Babel Tower Hypothesis explains the evolution of multilingual capabilities in LLMs, and optimizing the pre-training data distribution based on this hypothesis significantly improves multilingual performance.
papers.key_findings:
The performance of a new language during pre-training follows three stages: translation (reliance on dominant language), transition, and stabilization (use of own language-specific system).
For some languages, relying on a strong dominant language for translation is more effective than building a new knowledge system with additional data.
The internal state of the LLM, measured via working languages and language-transferring neurons, shifts from the dominant language system to the new language system over training.
Adjusting the pre-training data distribution allows different languages to reach their optimal performance state concurrently.
A method to estimate the optimal pre-training corpus distribution based on training loss and performance leads to models that outperform those trained on the original corpus.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to code languages and smaller models; future work should extend to natural languages and larger models.
future_direction: Extend the approach to natural language scenarios.
Scale to larger models.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown significant multilingual capabilities. However, the mechanisms underlying the development of these capabilities during pre-training are not well understood. In this paper, we use code LLMs as an experimental platform to explore the evolution of multilingual capabilities in LLMs during the pre-training process. Based on our observations, we propose the Babel Tower Hypothesis, which describes the entire process of LLMs acquiring new language capabilities. During the learning process, multiple languages initially share a single knowledge system dominated by the primary language and gradually develop language-specific knowledge systems. We then validate the above hypothesis by tracking the internal states of the LLMs through identifying working languages and language transferring neurons. Experimental results show that the internal state changes of the LLM are consistent with our Babel Tower Hypothesis. Building on these insights, we propose a novel method to construct an optimized pre-training corpus for multilingual code LLMs, which significantly outperforms LLMs trained on the original corpus. The proposed Babel Tower Hypothesis provides new insights into designing pre-training data distributions to achieve optimal multilingual capabilities in LLMs.

papers.title: Lost in Multilinguality: Dissecting Cross-lingual Factual Inconsistency in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the underlying causes of cross-lingual factual inconsistency in multilingual language models, and how can this inconsistency be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies that cross-lingual factual inconsistency in multilingual language models arises from failures in the language transition phase in the final layers, and proposes a linear shortcut method that bypasses these layers to improve both prediction accuracy and cross-lingual consistency.
papers.conclusion: Language transition errors are a key cause of cross-lingual inconsistency, and the proposed linear shortcut method effectively mitigates this issue, improving model consistency and accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
Multilingual language models encode factual knowledge in a language-independent concept space through most layers, transitioning to language-specific spaces only in the final layers.
Incorrect predictions in the target language often occur due to failures during the language transition, even when the correct answer is present in the concept space.
The proposed linear shortcut method, which bypasses final-layer computations, enhances prediction accuracy and cross-lingual consistency.
The concept space in LLaMA2 is English-centric, while BLOOM's concept space is more linguistically diverse.
The knowledge recall process in multilingual models involves three stages: relation processing, object extraction in the latent language, and language-specific adaptation.
papers.limitation:
The analysis assumes English as the pivot language, which may limit applicability to language pairs that do not involve English.
The KLAR dataset covers 17 languages but does not fully capture the diversity of world languages.
The shortcut method relies on linear approximation; non-linear approaches might better capture complex transformations.
The study does not explore downstream applications such as multilingual knowledge localization or editing.
future_direction: Expand the investigation to more languages and additional language models to assess broader applicability.
Develop non-linear shortcut methods to better mitigate language transition errors.
papers.abstract: Multilingual language models (MLMs) store factual knowledge across languages but often struggle to provide consistent responses to semantically equivalent prompts in different languages. While previous studies point out this cross-lingual inconsistency issue, the underlying causes remain unexplored. In this work, we use mechanistic interpretability methods to investigate cross-lingual inconsistencies in MLMs. We find that MLMs encode knowledge in a language-independent concept space through most layers, and only transition to language-specific spaces in the final layers. Failures during the language transition often result in incorrect predictions in the target language, even when the answers are correct in other languages. To mitigate this inconsistency issue, we propose a linear shortcut method that bypasses computations in the final layers, enhancing both prediction accuracy and cross-lingual consistency. Our findings shed light on the internal mechanisms of MLMs and provide a lightweight, effective strategy for producing more consistent factual outputs.

papers.title: Not All Language Model Features Are One-Dimensionally Linear
papers.research_question: Are some language model representations inherently multi-dimensional, and if so, how are these irreducible multi-dimensional features used in computation?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that language models learn irreducible multi-dimensional features (e.g., circular representations for days of the week and months of the year) and provides evidence that these features are the fundamental unit of computation for modular arithmetic tasks.
papers.conclusion: Understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary for a complete mechanistic decomposition of some language model behaviors, challenging the strict one-dimensional linear representation hypothesis.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders can automatically discover interpretable multi-dimensional features in language models, such as circular representations for days of the week and months of the year.
These circular features are irreducible according to formal separability and mixture indices, meaning they cannot be decomposed into independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features.
Models like Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B use these exact circular representations when solving modular arithmetic problems involving days and months.
Intervention experiments (subspace patching) show that the circular representations are causally involved in the model's computation for these tasks.
The circular representations respect a continuous notion of time, as shown by interventions with phrases like 'early Monday' and 'late Monday'.
papers.abstract: Recent work has proposed that language models perform computation by manipulating one-dimensional representations of concepts ("features") in activation space. In contrast, we explore whether some language model representations may be inherently multi-dimensional. We begin by developing a rigorous definition of irreducible multi-dimensional features based on whether they can be decomposed into either independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features. Motivated by these definitions, we design a scalable method that uses sparse autoencoders to automatically find multi-dimensional features in GPT-2 and Mistral 7B. These auto-discovered features include strikingly interpretable examples, e.g. circular features representing days of the week and months of the year. We identify tasks where these exact circles are used to solve computational problems involving modular arithmetic in days of the week and months of the year. Next, we provide evidence that these circular features are indeed the fundamental unit of computation in these tasks with intervention experiments on Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B, and we examine the continuity of the days of the week feature in Mistral 7B. Overall, our work argues that understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary to mechanistically decompose some model behaviors.

papers.title: Putting a Face to Forgetting: Continual Learning meets Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: How can catastrophic forgetting in continual learning be understood at a mechanistic level in terms of transformations to individual features?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a mechanistic framework that interprets catastrophic forgetting in continual learning as rotations and scalings of feature vectors, leading to capacity degradation and readout misalignment.
papers.conclusion: The framework provides a new vocabulary for diagnosing continual learning failures and shows that fading and misalignment are key drivers of forgetting.
papers.key_findings:
Forgetting is driven by rotations and scalings of feature vectors, which reduce allocated capacity and cause readout misalignment.
Worst-case forgetting occurs when tasks share features but with misaligned probes, leading to overlap and fading.
Depth worsens forgetting by increasing fading and overlap.
In a practical Vision Transformer, forgetting is driven more by fading and readout misalignment than by overlap.
Crosscoders can be used to track feature evolution in continual learning.
papers.limitation:
The tractable model assumes fixed probes, which exaggerates forgetting.
Crosscoder features are approximations and not ground-truth.
future_direction: Formal analysis of the effect of depth on feature norms and rotations.
Leveraging faded late-layer features identified at earlier layers to mitigate forgetting.
papers.abstract: Catastrophic forgetting in continual learning is often measured at the performance or last-layer representation level, overlooking the underlying mechanisms. We introduce a mechanistic framework that offers a geometric interpretation of catastrophic forgetting as the result of transformations to the encoding of individual features. These transformations can lead to forgetting by reducing the allocated capacity of features (worse representation) and disrupting their readout by downstream computations. Analysis of a tractable model formalizes this view, allowing us to identify best- and worst-case scenarios. Through experiments on this model, we empirically test our formal analysis and highlight the detrimental effect of depth. Finally, we demonstrate how our framework can be used in the analysis of practical models through the use of Crosscoders. We present a case study of a Vision Transformer trained on sequential CIFAR-10. Our work provides a new, feature-centric vocabulary for continual learning.

papers.title: False Friends Are Not Foes: Investigating Vocabulary Overlap in Multilingual Language Models
papers.research_question: Does token overlap facilitate cross-lingual transfer or introduce interference between languages? When and how does the presence of overlapping tokens improve cross-lingual transfer?
papers.core_contribution: Token overlap in multilingual models promotes cross-lingual semantic alignment and improves transfer performance, with semantically similar overlap being most beneficial.
papers.conclusion: Vocabulary overlap is advantageous for cross-lingual transfer, and tokenizer design should focus on other quality factors rather than reducing overlap.
papers.key_findings:
Models with any vocabulary overlap consistently outperform models with no overlap on XNLI and XQuAD tasks.
Transfer performance generally improves as overlap increases.
Tokens with high semantic similarity across languages contribute most to transfer performance.
Overlap enables embedding spaces to capture cross-lingual semantic relationships, an effect weaker in disjoint vocabularies.
The benefits of overlap vary with typological distance between languages, with high-similarity overlap being more critical for distant pairs.
papers.limitation:
Computational expense limits the number of language pairs studied.
Focus on English-centric language pairs may not generalize to non-English scenarios.
Use of a single tokenizer (XLM-R) may not capture effects of different tokenizer designs.
future_direction: Explore additional language pairs, particularly low-resource languages.
Investigate overlap effects in non-English language pairings.
Examine how overlap interacts with different tokenizers or extended training budgets.
papers.abstract: Subword tokenizers trained on multilingual corpora naturally produce overlapping tokens across languages. Does token overlap facilitate cross-lingual transfer or instead introduce interference between languages? Prior work offers mixed evidence, partly due to varied setups and confounders, such as token frequency or subword segmentation granularity. To address this question, we devise a controlled experiment where we train bilingual autoregressive models on multiple language pairs under systematically varied vocabulary overlap settings. Crucially, we explore a new dimension to understanding how overlap affects transfer: the semantic similarity of tokens shared across languages. We first analyze our models' hidden representations and find that overlap of any kind creates embedding spaces that capture cross-lingual semantic relationships, while this effect is much weaker in models with disjoint vocabularies. On XNLI and XQuAD, we find that models with overlap outperform models with disjoint vocabularies, and that transfer performance generally improves as overlap increases. Overall, our findings highlight the advantages of token overlap in multilingual models and show that substantial shared vocabulary remains a beneficial design choice for multilingual tokenizers.

papers.title: Roles and Utilization of Attention Heads in Transformer-based Neural Language Models
papers.research_question: How are basic linguistic properties captured with the attention heads across transformer-based models and used for downstream tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes an analysis method to understand where linguistic properties are learned and represented in attention heads of transformer architectures, and shows that selecting and concatenating influential attention heads can improve performance on downstream tasks.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that understanding the roles of attention heads can lead to adaptive sentence representations that improve downstream task performance, and reveals internal behaviors of transformer models during fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
Different attention heads on different layers are specialized for different linguistic properties (syntactic, semantic, surface).
The last layer of transformer encoders is not always the best for representing linguistic properties; earlier layers often dominate.
Concatenating the outputs of the top-n influential attention heads (selected via probing) yields better sentence representations and improves downstream task performance.
During fine-tuning, the initial superior attention heads remain influential and their performance is amplified, while adjacent heads also show increased performance.
Attention heads handle both syntactic and semantic information in a balanced way, with a linear relationship between their syntactic and semantic scores.
future_direction: Investigation of how heat maps vary during extensive pre-training to understand the dynamics of the learning processes.
papers.abstract: Sentence encoders based on the transformer architecture have shown promising results on various natural language tasks. The main impetus lies in the pre-trained neural language models that capture long-range dependencies among words, owing to multi-head attention that is unique in the architecture. However, little is known for how linguistic properties are processed, represented, and utilized for downstream tasks among hundreds of attention heads inside the pre-trained transformerbased model. For the initial goal of examining the roles of attention heads in handling a set of linguistic features, we conducted a set of experiments with ten probing tasks and three downstream tasks on four pre-trained transformer families (GPT, GPT2, BERT, and ELECTRA). Meaningful insights are shown through the lens of heat map visualization and utilized to propose a relatively simple sentence representation method that takes advantage of most influential attention heads, resulting in additional performance improvements on the downstream tasks.

papers.title: The Low-Dimensional Linear Geometry of Contextualized Word Representations
papers.research_question: How are linguistic features encoded in the linear geometry of contextualized word representations, and what are the geometric properties of these encodings?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that linguistic features are encoded in low-dimensional linear subspaces of contextualized word representations, that these subspaces have hierarchical structure and are distributed across neurons, and that they are causally relevant to model behavior.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a probing procedure that reveals low-dimensional linear subspaces encoding linguistic features in word representations, with hierarchical and distributed structure, and shows these subspaces are causally relevant to model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Linguistic features are encoded in low-dimensional subspaces of contextualized word representations.
These subspaces exhibit hierarchical structure (e.g., noun and verb subspaces nested within part-of-speech subspaces).
The subspaces are distributed across neurons rather than aligned with individual axes.
Ablating specific subspaces (e.g., nounspace or verbspace) impairs BERT's performance on subject-verb agreement, indicating causal relevance.
Contextual representations encode linguistic variables better but not more compactly than non-contextual word embeddings.
future_direction: Explore richer geometric structure in word representations and its effect on model behavior.
papers.abstract: Black-box probing models can reliably extract linguistic features like tense, number, and syntactic role from pretrained word representations. However, the manner in which these features are encoded in representations remains poorly understood. We present a systematic study of the linear geometry of contextualized word representations in ELMO and BERT. We show that a variety of linguistic features (including structured dependency relationships) are encoded in low-dimensional subspaces. We then refine this geometric picture, showing that there are hierarchical relations between the subspaces encoding general linguistic categories and more specific ones, and that lowdimensional feature encodings are distributed rather than aligned to individual neurons. Finally, we demonstrate that these linear subspaces are causally related to model behavior, and can be used to perform fine-grained manipulation of BERT's output distribution.

papers.title: Linguistic Minimal Pairs Elicit Linguistic Similarity in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do Large Language Models represent different linguistic phenomena, and are linguistically similar phenomena represented similarly in LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method using linguistic minimal pairs to measure linguistic similarity in LLMs, revealing that linguistic similarity is influenced by training data, aligns with fine-grained linguistic categories, weakly correlates with semantic similarity, and shows limited cross-lingual alignment.
papers.conclusion: The work provides insights into LLMs' internal language processing, bridging neural models and linguistic theory, and offers a foundation for future research.
papers.key_findings:
Linguistic similarity is significantly influenced by training data exposure, leading to higher cross-LLM agreement in higher-resource languages.
Linguistic similarity strongly aligns with fine-grained theoretical linguistic categories but weakly with broader ones.
Linguistic similarity shows a weak correlation with semantic similarity, indicating its context-dependent nature.
LLMs exhibit limited cross-lingual alignment in their understanding of relevant linguistic phenomena.
papers.limitation:
Dependent on the quality and scope of existing linguistic minimal pair datasets
Limited to three languages, not representing global linguistic diversity
Only captures a fraction of language's complexity with 150 phenomena
future_direction: Developing more high-quality minimal pairs
Broadening language coverage to include more diverse linguistic families
Increasing the range of phenomena studied
papers.abstract: We introduce a novel analysis that leverages linguistic minimal pairs to probe the internal linguistic representations of Large Language Models (LLMs). By measuring the similarity between LLM activation differences across minimal pairs, we quantify the and gain insight into the linguistic knowledge captured by LLMs. Our large-scale experiments, spanning 100+ LLMs and 150k minimal pairs in three languages, reveal properties of linguistic similarity from four key aspects: consistency across LLMs, relation to theoretical categorizations, dependency to semantic context, and cross-lingual alignment of relevant phenomena. Our findings suggest that 1) linguistic similarity is significantly influenced by training data exposure, leading to higher cross-LLM agreement in higher-resource languages. 2) Linguistic similarity strongly aligns with fine-grained theoretical linguistic categories but weakly with broader ones. 3) Linguistic similarity shows a weak correlation with semantic similarity, showing its context-dependent nature. 4) LLMs exhibit limited cross-lingual alignment in their understanding of relevant linguistic phenomena. This work demonstrates the potential of minimal pairs as a window into the neural representations of language in LLMs, shedding light on the relationship between LLMs and linguistic theory. Codes and data are available at https://github.com/ChenDelong1999/Linguistic-Similarity

papers.title: Knowledge Accumulation in Continually Learned Representations and the Issue of Feature Forgetting
papers.research_question: Do continually trained representations forget catastrophically? What are the consequences of forgetting these representations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that, when measured relative to performance gained during a task, forgetting in continually learned representations is as catastrophic as at the output level, except for information shared across tasks. It also demonstrates that this feature forgetting substantially hinders the accumulation of general knowledge.
papers.conclusion: Representations in continually trained neural networks forget catastrophically when considering relative forgetting, and this feature forgetting impedes the efficient accumulation of general knowledge. Preventing feature forgetting is crucial for learning strong representations over time.
papers.key_findings:
Continually learned representations exhibit two key phenomena: feature forgetting (loss of task-specific information) and knowledge accumulation (improvement on unseen tasks).
Relative forgetting (forgetting relative to performance gained during a task) reveals that representations forget newly learned information as catastrophically as the output layer, except for the first few tasks.
Information that is not forgotten from early tasks is information that is shared and can be re-learned from later tasks, as shown by task exclusion experiments.
Feature forgetting slows down knowledge accumulation, as demonstrated by an ensemble baseline that avoids forgetting and achieves much better general representations.
Among continual learning methods, functional regularization (e.g., MAS, LwF) is most effective at reducing feature forgetting and promoting knowledge accumulation.
papers.abstract: Continual learning research has shown that neural networks suffer from catastrophic forgetting "at the output level", but it is debated whether this is also the case at the level of learned representations. Multiple recent studies ascribe representations a certain level of innate robustness against forgetting -- that they only forget minimally in comparison with forgetting at the output level. We revisit and expand upon the experiments that revealed this difference in forgetting and illustrate the coexistence of two phenomena that affect the quality of continually learned representations: knowledge accumulation and feature forgetting. Taking both aspects into account, we show that, even though forgetting in the representation (i.e. feature forgetting) can be small in absolute terms, when measuring relative to how much was learned during a task, forgetting in the representation tends to be just as catastrophic as forgetting at the output level. Next we show that this feature forgetting is problematic as it substantially slows down the incremental learning of good general representations (i.e. knowledge accumulation). Finally, we study how feature forgetting and knowledge accumulation are affected by different types of continual learning methods.

papers.title: Transformer Language Models without Positional Encodings Still Learn Positional Information
papers.research_question: Can transformer language models learn positional information without explicit positional encodings, and how do they do it?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer language models without explicit positional encodings (NoPos) can learn implicit positional information and achieve competitive performance, and this ability is due to the causal attention mask.
papers.conclusion: Transformer language models can learn positional information without explicit encodings, and this phenomenon is robust across settings but does not extend to masked language models, with the causal attention mechanism being the key factor.
papers.key_findings:
NoPos models achieve competitive perplexity compared to models with explicit positional encodings across different datasets, model sizes, and sequence lengths.
Probing experiments show that NoPos models learn an implicit notion of absolute positions in their hidden representations, similar to models with learned positional embeddings.
The success of NoPos models is unique to causal language models; masked language models fail to converge without positional encodings.
Shuffling the prefix tokens leads to a dramatic increase in loss, indicating that the model uses the learned positional information.
The causal attention mask is conjectured to allow the model to infer absolute positions by counting the number of attendable tokens.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are limited to models up to 1.3B parameters, and while the trend suggests the findings should hold for larger models, this is not tested.
NoPos models are always slightly worse than models with positional encodings, indicating that the inductive bias of positional encoding is important.
papers.abstract: Causal transformer language models (LMs), such as GPT-3, typically require some form of positional encoding, such as positional embeddings. However, we show that LMs without any explicit positional encoding are still competitive with standard models and that this phenomenon is robust across different datasets, model sizes, and sequence lengths.Probing experiments reveal that such models acquire an implicit notion of absolute positions throughout the network, effectively compensating for the missing information.We conjecture that causal attention enables the model to infer the number of predecessors that each token can attend to, thereby approximating its absolute position.Our findings indicate that causal LMs might derive positional awareness not only from the explicit positioning mechanism but also from the effects of the causal mask.

papers.title: Encourage or Inhibit Monosemanticity? Revisit Monosemanticity from a Feature Decorrelation Perspective
papers.research_question: Should monosemanticity be encouraged or inhibited for LLM's alignment?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that monosemanticity is positively correlated with model capacity during preference alignment and proposes a feature decorrelation regularizer (DecPO) that enhances monosemanticity and improves alignment performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper provides empirical evidence that alignment (e.g., DPO) improves monosemanticity and that enhancing monosemanticity via a decorrelation regularizer (DecPO) leads to better model capacity and alignment performance.
papers.key_findings:
DPO training improves monosemanticity, especially in earlier model layers.
Feature decorrelation is a reliable proxy for monosemanticity within a single model.
The proposed DecPO regularizer enhances feature decorrelation and activation sparsity.
DecPO improves preference alignment performance over DPO and other baselines across multiple datasets.
DecPO leads to larger reward margins during training, indicating better capture of diverse features.
papers.limitation:
Much of the analysis is ad hoc, tailored to specific features, and requires substantial researcher effort.
Models studied are all from the same Llama family and trained with limited data; the largest model is Llama3-8b, which is far from the frontier, so analysis may miss dynamics in larger models.
papers.abstract: To better interpret the intrinsic mechanism of large language models (LLMs), recent studies focus on monosemanticity on its basic units. A monosemantic neuron is dedicated to a single and specific concept, which forms a one-to-one correlation between neurons and concepts. Despite extensive research in monosemanticity probing, it remains unclear whether monosemanticity is beneficial or harmful to model capacity. To explore this question, we revisit monosemanticity from the feature decorrelation perspective and advocate for its encouragement. We experimentally observe that the current conclusion by wang2024learning, which suggests that decreasing monosemanticity enhances model performance, does not hold when the model changes. Instead, we demonstrate that monosemanticity consistently exhibits a positive correlation with model capacity, in the preference alignment process. Consequently, we apply feature correlation as a proxy for monosemanticity and incorporate a feature decorrelation regularizer into the dynamic preference optimization process. The experiments show that our method not only enhances representation diversity and activation sparsity but also improves preference alignment performance.

papers.title: Discriminating Form and Meaning in Multilingual Models with Minimal-Pair ABX Tasks
papers.research_question: How do multilingual language models represent language identity (form) and semantic content (meaning), and how do these representations evolve during training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a training-free ABX-style discrimination framework for analyzing multilingual representations, and shows that in XLM-R, language discrimination decreases and concentrates in lower layers over training, while meaning discrimination increases and stabilizes in deeper layers.
papers.conclusion: ABX discrimination metrics provide a lightweight, interpretable tool for analyzing multilingual representations, revealing that language discrimination decreases and concentrates in lower layers while meaning discrimination increases in deeper layers, with implications for understanding cross-lingual transfer.
papers.key_findings:
Language discrimination declines over training and becomes concentrated in lower layers.
Meaning discrimination strengthens over time and stabilizes in deeper layers.
There is a negative correlation between language and meaning discrimination across language pairs and checkpoints.
Language discrimination negatively correlates with performance on form-sensitive tasks like POS and NER in cross-lingual transfer.
Meaning discrimination does not consistently predict downstream task performance.
papers.limitation:
Encoder architecture and single-model scope: only tested on XLM-R (encoder-only), not decoder-only or encoder-decoder models.
Discrimination vs Separation: does not explicitly quantify separation in the representation space.
Task coverage: only POS, NER, NLI, may not capture deeper semantic capabilities.
Cross-linguistic generality vs. language-specific phenomena: not investigating specific languages or families in detail.
future_direction: Linking discrimination patterns to typological linguistic features.
Evaluating deeper semantic tasks.
Applying ABX metrics to decoder-only LLMs and more recent multilingual models.
papers.abstract: We introduce a set of training-free ABX-style discrimination tasks to evaluate how multilingual language models represent language identity (form) and semantic content (meaning). Inspired from speech processing, these zero-shot tasks measure whether minimal differences in representation can be reliably detected. This offers a flexible and interpretable alternative to probing. Applied to XLM-R (Conneau et al, 2020) across pretraining checkpoints and layers, we find that language discrimination declines over training and becomes concentrated in lower layers, while meaning discrimination strengthens over time and stabilizes in deeper layers. We then explore probing tasks, showing some alignment between our metrics and linguistic learning performance. Our results position ABX tasks as a lightweight framework for analyzing the structure of multilingual representations.

papers.title: Viewing Knowledge Transfer in Multilingual Machine Translation Through a Representational Lens
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between cross-lingual knowledge transfer and representational similarities in multilingual neural machine translation, and can we develop a better measure for transfer than translation quality alone?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Representational Transfer Potential (RTP), a measure of knowledge transfer based on representational similarities between languages in multilingual machine translation, and proposes a novel training scheme with an auxiliary similarity loss that improves translation quality for low- and mid-resource languages.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that Representational Transfer Potential (RTP) is a better measure of knowledge transfer than translation quality alone, and that explicitly optimizing for language invariance using multi-parallel data improves translation for low-resource languages.
papers.key_findings:
Representational Transfer Potential (RTP) can measure both positive and negative transfer and is strongly correlated with changes in translation quality (BLEU), indicating that improvements are due to knowledge transfer and not just increased target data.
Multi-parallel overlap between languages is a highly predictive yet under-explored feature for transfer.
A training method that uses an auxiliary similarity loss to encourage language-invariant representations yields increased translation quality for low- and mid-resource languages across multiple data and model setups.
RTP can be used to identify suitable auxiliary transfer languages, with training on top RTP contributors leading to substantially better results than training on bottom contributors.
Dataset features (multi-parallel overlap, source subword overlap, vocabulary occupancy) are more predictive of representational similarity than linguistic features.
papers.limitation:
The analysis focuses on English-centric many-to-many and many-to-English models, which may limit the generalizability of the results to other multilingual settings.
The training data size (TED corpus) is relatively small compared to other datasets like OPUS-100, which may affect model performance.
papers.abstract: We argue that translation quality alone is not a sufficient metric for measuring knowledge transfer in multilingual neural machine translation. To support this claim, we introduce Representational Transfer Potential (RTP), which measures representational similarities between languages. We show that RTP can measure both positive and negative transfer (interference), and find that RTP is strongly correlated with changes in translation quality, indicating that transfer does occur. Furthermore, we investigate data and language characteristics that are relevant for transfer, and find that multi-parallel overlap is an important yet under-explored feature. Based on this, we develop a novel training scheme, which uses an auxiliary similarity loss that encourages representations to be more invariant across languages by taking advantage of multi-parallel data. We show that our method yields increased translation quality for low- and mid-resource languages across multiple data and model setups.

papers.title: When Alignment Hurts: Decoupling Representational Spaces in Multilingual Models
papers.research_question: Does alignment with a high-resource standard language always benefit related low-resource varieties? The paper challenges this assumption by showing that excessive representational entanglement can hinder generative modeling.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an online variational probing framework for subspace decoupling, providing causal evidence that representational entanglement with a high-resource language hinders generative modeling for low-resource varieties.
papers.conclusion: This work demonstrates that representational entanglement with a high-resource language is a critical and addressable bottleneck for generative modeling in closely-related, low-resource language varieties, and provides a causal intervention method to mitigate it.
papers.key_findings:
Excessive representational entanglement with Modern Standard Arabic (MSA) hinders generative performance for low-resource Arabic dialects.
Better generative performance correlates with greater representational separability from MSA in the model's internal geometry.
The proposed online subspace decoupling intervention improves dialectal generation by up to +4.9 chrF++ on individual dialects and +2.0 on average compared to standard fine-tuning.
The intervention leads to a trade-off, with a measured decrease in standard-language (MSA) generation performance.
The method is effective across 25 Arabic dialects, demonstrating the generalizability of the representational dominance phenomenon.
papers.limitation:
The MADAR dataset is composed of relatively short sentences, which may not fully capture model behaviors on tasks requiring longer-form generation.
The causal claim is based on intervention experiments within a single language family (Arabic), and generalization to other language families requires further validation.
future_direction: Scalable and Efficient Methods
Inference-Time Interventions
Generalization to Other Languages
papers.abstract: Alignment with high-resource standard languages is often assumed to aid the modeling of related low-resource varieties. We challenge this assumption by demonstrating that excessive representational entanglement with a dominant variety, such as Modern Standard Arabic (MSA) in relation to Arabic dialects, can actively hinder generative modeling. We present the first comprehensive causal study of this phenomenon by analyzing and directly intervening in the internal representation geometry of large language models (LLMs). Our key contribution is an online variational probing framework that continuously estimates the subspace of the standard variety during fine-tuning, enabling projection-based decoupling from this space. While our study uses Arabic as a case due to its unusually rich parallel resources across 25 dialects, the broader motivation is methodological: dialectal MT serves as a controlled proxy for generative tasks where comparable multi-variety corpora are unavailable. Across 25 dialects, our intervention improves generation quality by up to +4.9 chrF++ and +2.0 on average compared to standard fine-tuning, despite a measured tradeoff in standard-language performance. These results provide causal evidence that subspace dominance by high-resource varieties can restrict generative capacity for related varieties. More generally, we unify geometric and information-theoretic probing with subspace-level causal interventions, offering practical tools for improving generative modeling in closely related language families and, more broadly, for controlling representational allocation in multilingual and multi-domain LLMs. Code will be released.

papers.title: Improving Zero-Shot Translation by Disentangling Positional Information
papers.research_question: What is a main factor causing language-specific representations in multilingual NMT that hinders zero-shot translation, and how can it be alleviated?
papers.core_contribution: Removing residual connections in a middle encoder layer improves zero-shot translation by reducing positional correspondence to input tokens, leading to more language-independent representations.
papers.conclusion: Positional correspondence to input tokens hinders zero-shot translation, and removing residual connections in a middle encoder layer alleviates this issue, leading to improved zero-shot performance and more language-independent representations.
papers.key_findings:
Removing residual connections in a middle encoder layer substantially improves zero-shot translation BLEU scores (up to 18.5 points gain).
The improvement is particularly prominent between related languages, where the proposed model outperforms pivot-based translation.
The approach allows easy integration of new languages, enabling zero-shot translation between the new language and all previously trained languages.
Analysis shows the proposed model creates encoder outputs with less positional correspondence and higher language independence, as measured by classification accuracy and SVCCA.
In low-resource, low lexical overlap settings (PMIndia), combining residual removal with variational dropout is essential for achieving reasonable zero-shot performance.
papers.limitation: The method requires additional regularization (variational dropout) to achieve reasonable zero-shot performance in low-resource settings with little lexical overlap (e.g., PMIndia).
papers.abstract: Multilingual neural machine translation has shown the capability of directly translating between language pairs unseen in training, i.e. zero-shot translation. Despite being conceptually attractive, it often suffers from low output quality. The difficulty of generalizing to new translation directions suggests the model representations are highly specific to those language pairs seen in training. We demonstrate that a main factor causing the language-specific representations is the positional correspondence to input tokens. We show that this can be easily alleviated by removing residual connections in an encoder layer. With this modification, we gain up to 18.5 BLEU points on zero-shot translation while retaining quality on supervised directions. The improvements are particularly prominent between related languages, where our proposed model outperforms pivot-based translation. Moreover, our approach allows easy integration of new languages, which substantially expands translation coverage. By thorough inspections of the hidden layer outputs, we show that our approach indeed leads to more language-independent representations.

papers.title: Shape or Texture: Understanding Discriminative Features in CNNs
papers.research_question: What type of shape information is discriminative in CNNs, where is shape information encoded, and when does the network learn about object shape during training?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that CNNs learn shape information early in training, encode it primarily in the last few layers, and that shape encoding does not guarantee per-pixel semantic understanding.
papers.conclusion: The paper provides a systematic study of shape encoding in CNNs, revealing important mechanisms that characterize a network's ability to encode shape information, which can inform the design of more robust and trustworthy computer vision algorithms.
papers.key_findings:
CNNs learn the majority of shape information during the first few epochs of training.
Shape information is largely encoded in the last few layers of a CNN.
Biasing a CNN towards shape changes the number of shape encoding neurons in the last feature encoding stage.
Early layers also encode shape information, which can be combined with deeper layers for better shape extraction.
Encoding shape does not imply the encoding of localized per-pixel semantic information.
papers.abstract: Contrasting the previous evidence that neurons in the later layers of a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) respond to complex object shapes, recent studies have shown that CNNs actually exhibit a `texture bias': given an image with both texture and shape cues (e.g., a stylized image), a CNN is biased towards predicting the category corresponding to the texture. However, these previous studies conduct experiments on the final classification output of the network, and fail to robustly evaluate the bias contained (i) in the latent representations, and (ii) on a per-pixel level. In this paper, we design a series of experiments that overcome these issues. We do this with the goal of better understanding what type of shape information contained in the network is discriminative, where shape information is encoded, as well as when the network learns about object shape during training. We show that a network learns the majority of overall shape information at the first few epochs of training and that this information is largely encoded in the last few layers of a CNN. Finally, we show that the encoding of shape does not imply the encoding of localized per-pixel semantic information. The experimental results and findings provide a more accurate understanding of the behaviour of current CNNs, thus helping to inform future design choices.

papers.title: Copy Suppression: Comprehensively Understanding an Attention Head
papers.research_question: What is the main role of attention head L10H7 in GPT-2 Small across the entire training distribution?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies and explains the copy suppression mechanism of attention head L10H7 in GPT-2 Small, showing it suppresses naive copying to improve calibration and accounts for 76.9% of the head's impact.
papers.conclusion: The paper introduces copy suppression as the main role of attention head L10H7 in GPT-2 Small and verifies it mechanistically using weights-based analysis of QK and OV circuits, providing a comprehensive explanation of a component in a language model.
papers.key_findings:
The main role of attention head L10H7 in GPT-2 Small is copy suppression, which explains 76.9% of its behavior on the training distribution.
Copy suppression reduces model loss and improves calibration by suppressing incorrect token predictions that appear earlier in context.
Copy suppression is a mechanism for self-repair, explaining 39% of self-repair in the Indirect Object Identification (IOI) task.
The OV circuit of L10H7 suppresses the tokens it attends to, with 84.70% of tokens having their diagonal as one of the top 10 most negative values.
The QK circuit of L10H7 attends to tokens that are predicted at the query position, with 95.72% of diagonal values being the largest in their rows.
papers.limitation:
The idealised setup for analyzing the QK circuit does not completely faithfully represent L10H7's real functioning.
Using KL divergence as an ablation metric has limitations, as discussed in Appendix J.
papers.abstract: We present a single attention head in GPT-2 Small that has one main role across the entire training distribution. If components in earlier layers predict a certain token, and this token appears earlier in the context, the head suppresses it: we call this copy suppression. Attention Head 10.7 (L10H7) suppresses naive copying behavior which improves overall model calibration. This explains why multiple prior works studying certain narrow tasks found negative heads that systematically favored the wrong answer. We uncover the mechanism that the Negative Heads use for copy suppression with weights-based evidence and are able to explain 76.9% of the impact of L10H7 in GPT-2 Small. To the best of our knowledge, this is the most comprehensive description of the complete role of a component in a language model to date.
