papers.title: Isolating Culture Neurons in Multilingual Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Can we localize a set of neurons that drives cultural propensities in multilingual LLMs, separate them from language-specific neurons, and modulate them through interventions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that culture-specific neurons can be identified in multilingual LLMs, are largely separable from language-specific neurons, and can be selectively modulated through interventions.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that cultural knowledge concentrates in specialized neuron populations predominantly localized in upper layers of multilingual language models and that pure culture neurons play a substantial functional role.
papers.key_findings:
Culture-specific neurons are largely separable from language-specific neurons.
Cultural representations are localized in upper layers of the model.
Different cultures are encoded in distinct neural populations with minimal cross-cultural interference.
Pure culture-specific neurons (not overlapping with language) constitute about 56.7% of culture-related neurons and are functionally important.
Ablation of culture-specific neurons increases perplexity on culturally relevant data, confirming their critical role.
papers.limitation:
Analysis restricted to a small set of open-source models.
Methodology relies on entropy-based metrics and dataset sampling choices.
MUREL covers only six cultures, potentially omitting important cultural phenomena.
Evaluation focuses on neuron ablation and perplexity; future work should include more comprehensive behavioral and downstream assessments.
future_direction: Broadening coverage to additional cultures, languages, and models.
Extending localization to attention heads.
Testing sufficiency via activation scaling and steering, and evaluating intervention effects on downstream tasks.
papers.abstract: Language and culture are deeply intertwined, yet it has been unclear how and where multilingual large language models encode culture. Here, we build on an established methodology for identifying language-specific neurons to localize and isolate culture-specific neurons, carefully disentangling their overlap and interaction with language-specific neurons. To facilitate our experiments, we introduce MUREL, a curated dataset of 85.2 million tokens spanning six different cultures. Our localization and intervention experiments show that LLMs encode different cultures in distinct neuron populations, predominantly in upper layers, and that these culture neurons can be modulated largely independently of language-specific neurons or those specific to other cultures. These findings suggest that cultural knowledge and propensities in multilingual language models can be selectively isolated and edited, with implications for fairness, inclusivity, and alignment. Code and data are available at https://github.com/namazifard/Culture_Neurons.

papers.title: How multilingual is Multilingual BERT?
papers.research_question: Why is Multilingual BERT (M-BERT) effective at zero-shot cross-lingual model transfer?
papers.core_contribution: M-BERT learns multilingual representations from monolingual corpora, enabling zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, but transfer effectiveness depends on typological similarity and script consistency.
papers.conclusion: M-BERT's cross-lingual transfer ability is due to multilingual representations learned from monolingual data, but for full effectiveness across all language pairs, explicit multilingual training objectives are needed.
papers.key_findings:
M-BERT can perform cross-lingual transfer even between languages with different scripts, indicating deep multilingual representations beyond vocabulary memorization.
Transfer performance is higher for typologically similar languages, suggesting that the model maps structures but does not learn systematic transformations for different word orders.
M-BERT generalizes to code-switched text when trained on monolingual data, showing its multilingual representation capability.
The model struggles with transliterated text, indicating limitations in handling non-standard scripts without explicit training.
The feature space of M-BERT allows for finding translation pairs through vector arithmetic, demonstrating a shared multilingual subspace.
papers.limitation:
Transfer is less accurate for languages with different word orders, such as English and Japanese.
M-BERT does not generalize well to transliterated text without explicit transliteration signals.
future_direction: Incorporate explicit multilingual training objectives to improve transfer to typologically divergent and transliterated targets.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we show that Multilingual BERT (M-BERT), released by Devlin et al. (2018) as a single language model pre-trained from monolingual corpora in 104 languages, is surprisingly good at zero-shot cross-lingual model transfer, in which task-specific annotations in one language are used to fine-tune the model for evaluation in another language. To understand why, we present a large number of probing experiments, showing that transfer is possible even to languages in different scripts, that transfer works best between typologically similar languages, that monolingual corpora can train models for code-switching, and that the model can find translation pairs. From these results, we can conclude that M-BERT does create multilingual representations, but that these representations exhibit systematic deficiencies affecting certain language pairs.

papers.title: An Analysis of Encoder Representations in Transformer-Based Machine Translation
papers.research_question: What kind of linguistic information (syntactic and semantic) is learned by the encoder of Transformer-based machine translation models, and how does it vary across layers and models with different translation quality?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes encoder representations in Transformer-based machine translation and finds that specific attention heads capture syntactic dependencies, with lower layers encoding more syntax and higher layers more semantics.
papers.conclusion: The experimental evaluation sheds light on interesting findings about dependency relations and syntactic and semantic behavior across layers in Transformer encoder representations.
papers.key_findings:
Each layer has at least one attention head that encodes a significant amount of syntactic dependencies.
Lower layers tend to encode more syntactic information, while upper layers move towards semantic tasks.
The information about the length of the input sentence starts to vanish after the third layer.
Attention can be used to transfer knowledge between high- and low-resource languages, improving translation quality.
future_direction: Extend the analysis with probing tasks to evaluate other linguistic properties.
Use a recent evaluation dataset for analysis.
Analyze the attention weights between the encoder and the decoder.
papers.abstract: The attention mechanism is a successful technique in modern NLP, especially in tasks like machine translation. The recently proposed network architecture of the Transformer is based entirely on attention mechanisms and achieves new state of the art results in neural machine translation, outperforming other sequence-to-sequence models. However, so far not much is known about the internal properties of the model and the representations it learns to achieve that performance. To study this question, we investigate the information that is learned by the attention mechanism in Transformer models with different translation quality. We assess the representations of the encoder by extracting dependency relations based on self-attention weights, we perform four probing tasks to study the amount of syntactic and semantic captured information and we also test attention in a transfer learning scenario. Our analysis sheds light on the relative strengths and weaknesses of the various encoder representations. We observe that specific attention heads mark syntactic dependency relations and we can also confirm that lower layers tend to learn more about syntax while higher layers tend to encode more semantics.

papers.title: Understanding Cross-Lingual Syntactic Transfer in Multilingual Recurrent Neural Networks.
papers.research_question: Does exposure to a related language (L1) improve implicit syntactic knowledge in a target language (L2) within multilingual neural networks? Do these networks induce a common representation space with shared syntactic categories?
papers.core_contribution: Cross-lingual syntactic transfer in multilingual neural networks is limited and inconsistent, and optimal conditions for lexical-semantic transfer may not be optimal for syntactic transfer.
papers.conclusion: Transfer of purely grammatical knowledge is limited and dependent on language pairs, and modern multilingual neural networks are still far from acquiring a true interlingua.
papers.key_findings:
Exposing a model to a related language does not always improve grammatical knowledge in the target language; in some cases, it causes negative interference.
Transfer of purely grammatical knowledge (e.g., long-range agreement in nonce sentences) is very limited and strongly dependent on the specific source-target language pair.
Part-of-speech categories are shared to a moderate extent across languages in the models, but dependency categories are not shared at all.
Language relatedness is the most determining factor for both word embedding alignment and part-of-speech transfer.
Scaling from two to nine input languages improves part-of-speech transfer among related languages but worsens it between unrelated languages.
papers.limitation:
Transfer of syntactic knowledge is limited and inconsistent, with negative interference observed in some language pairs (e.g., French to Italian).
Syntactic knowledge transfer within the models is shallow, with dependency categories not shared across languages.
papers.abstract: It is now established that modern neural language models can be successfully trained on multiple languages simultaneously without changes to the underlying architecture. But what kind of knowledge is really shared among languages within these models? Does multilingual training mostly lead to an alignment of the lexical representation spaces or does it also enable the sharing of purely grammatical knowledge? In this paper we dissect different forms of cross-lingual transfer and look for its most determining factors, using a variety of models and probing tasks. We find that exposing our LMs to a related language does not always increase grammatical knowledge in the target language, and that optimal conditions for lexical-semantic transfer may not be optimal for syntactic transfer.

papers.title: Locating and Editing Factual Associations in GPT
papers.research_question: How are factual associations stored and recalled in autoregressive transformer language models, and can they be directly edited?
papers.core_contribution: Factual associations in GPT are stored in mid-layer feed-forward modules and can be directly edited using a rank-one update method (ROME), which achieves strong generalization and specificity.
papers.conclusion: Factual associations in autoregressive transformers are stored in mid-layer MLP modules and can be directly edited via localized weight updates, with ROME providing an effective method for such edits.
papers.key_findings:
Causal tracing reveals that mid-layer MLP modules at the last subject token are decisive for factual predictions.
The Rank-One Model Editing (ROME) method can effectively edit factual associations by updating a single MLP layer with a rank-one weight update.
ROME achieves strong generalization and specificity on counterfactual edits, outperforming previous fine-tuning and hypernetwork-based methods.
The early site (mid-layer MLP) and late site (late-layer attention) play different roles: MLP stores the association, and attention copies it to the output.
The paper introduces a new dataset, COUNTERFACT, for evaluating counterfactual model edits.
papers.limitation: Human evaluation reveals a reduction in fluency of generated text under ROME, which the automatic entropy measure does not capture.
papers.abstract: We analyze the storage and recall of factual associations in autoregressive transformer language models, finding evidence that these associations correspond to localized, directly-editable computations. We first develop a causal intervention for identifying neuron activations that are decisive in a model's factual predictions. This reveals a distinct set of steps in middle-layer feed-forward modules that mediate factual predictions while processing subject tokens. To test our hypothesis that these computations correspond to factual association recall, we modify feed-forward weights to update specific factual associations using Rank-One Model Editing (ROME). We find that ROME is effective on a standard zero-shot relation extraction (zsRE) model-editing task, comparable to existing methods. To perform a more sensitive evaluation, we also evaluate ROME on a new dataset of counterfactual assertions, on which it simultaneously maintains both specificity and generalization, whereas other methods sacrifice one or another. Our results confirm an important role for mid-layer feed-forward modules in storing factual associations and suggest that direct manipulation of computational mechanisms may be a feasible approach for model editing. The code, dataset, visualizations, and an interactive demo notebook are available at https://rome.baulab.info/

papers.title: Do Vision Transformers See Like Convolutional Neural Networks?
papers.research_question: How are Vision Transformers solving image tasks? Are they acting like convolutional networks, or learning entirely different visual representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds key representational differences between Vision Transformers (ViTs) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), showing ViTs have more uniform layer representations, incorporate global information earlier via self-attention, and have stronger skip connections that propagate features differently.
papers.conclusion: ViTs and CNNs have clear differences in features and internal structure, with ViTs using global features early and strong skip connections, while local information aggregation is learned from scratch at scale. ViTs show strong spatial localization, promising for future uses like object detection.
papers.key_findings:
ViTs have a more uniform internal representation structure with greater similarity between lower and higher layers compared to the staged similarity in ResNets.
ViTs incorporate global information in lower layers through self-attention, while CNNs are restricted to local receptive fields; this leads to quantitatively different features.
Skip connections in ViTs are more influential than in ResNets, with a phase transition: early layers strongly propagate the CLS token, while later layers propagate spatial token representations.
ViTs preserve input spatial information more faithfully than ResNets in higher layers, especially when trained with a CLS token rather than global average pooling.
Large-scale pretraining data is crucial for ViTs to learn to attend locally in early layers and to develop high-quality intermediate representations for transfer learning.
papers.limitation: The study uses CKA, which summarizes measurements into a single scalar; while complemented with interventional tests and linear probes, more fine-grained methods may reveal additional insights.
papers.abstract: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have so far been the de-facto model for visual data. Recent work has shown that (Vision) Transformer models (ViT) can achieve comparable or even superior performance on image classification tasks. This raises a central question: how are Vision Transformers solving these tasks? Are they acting like convolutional networks, or learning entirely different visual representations? Analyzing the internal representation structure of ViTs and CNNs on image classification benchmarks, we find striking differences between the two architectures, such as ViT having more uniform representations across all layers. We explore how these differences arise, finding crucial roles played by self-attention, which enables early aggregation of global information, and ViT residual connections, which strongly propagate features from lower to higher layers. We study the ramifications for spatial localization, demonstrating ViTs successfully preserve input spatial information, with noticeable effects from different classification methods. Finally, we study the effect of (pretraining) dataset scale on intermediate features and transfer learning, and conclude with a discussion on connections to new architectures such as the MLP-Mixer.

papers.title: Just Say No to Single Embeddings: Why Your AI Needs Multiple Perspectives
papers.research_question: How does BERT represent linguistic features internally, and what is the geometric structure of these representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that BERT represents linguistic features in separate semantic and syntactic subspaces, provides evidence of fine-grained geometric representation of word senses, and gives a mathematical argument for the squared-distance tree embedding.
papers.conclusion: The paper's experiments suggest that BERT's internal geometry consists of multiple linear subspaces for different syntactic and semantic information, and that understanding this geometry can help improve transformer architectures.
papers.key_findings:
Attention matrices encode syntactic dependency relations, as shown by linear probes achieving high accuracy.
Parse tree embeddings in BERT approximate Pythagorean embeddings (squared Euclidean distance corresponds to tree distance), and there is a mathematical justification for this.
Word senses are represented as clusters in embedding space, and a simple nearest-neighbor classifier on BERT embeddings achieves state-of-the-art word sense disambiguation.
Semantic information can be isolated in a lower-dimensional subspace via a learned linear transformation (semantic probe).
Concatenating sentences with different word senses can cause embeddings to shift towards the opposing sense, indicating that tokens absorb meaning from all neighboring tokens.
future_direction: Investigating other meaningful subspaces in BERT's internal geometry
Using internal geometry to improve or refine transformer architectures
papers.abstract: Note: This is a work in progress document We present empirical evidence that conversations exhibit consistent geometric signatures when projected into different embedding spaces, alongside surprising variability in local feature detection. Analyzing 229 multi-agent AI dialogues from our prior study on social dynamics [Garcia, 2025], we examine whether geometric properties of conversational trajectories remain consistent across 5 fundamentally different embedding models. Our analysis reveals a striking dichotomy: while global geometric patterns (distance matrices, trajectory shapes) show remarkable consistency across both transformer-based and classical embeddings (correlations ranging from 0.521 to 0.957), local phase detection exhibits extreme variability (F1 scores from 0.08 to 0.36, agreement correlations from -0.14 to 0.76). This pattern of high global consistency with low local agreement suggests that different embedding models may capture distinct projections of conversations existing in a higher-dimensional semantic space. Transport-based analysis supports this interpretation, showing threefold increases in cross-paradigm distances compared to within-paradigm distances. These findings establish that while geometric analysis of conversation captures genuine structural properties, the global-local dichotomy implies fundamental limits on fine-grained analysis and raises intriguing questions about the true dimensionality of conversational dynamics.

papers.title: Unraveling Babel: Exploring Multilingual Activation Patterns of LLMs and Their Applications
papers.research_question: How do the internal neuron activation patterns of LLMs differ when processing different languages, and how can these patterns be leveraged for applications like model pruning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to convert dense LLMs into fine-grained MoE architectures to study multilingual activation patterns, and uses these patterns to guide language-specific model pruning, reducing computation while maintaining or even improving performance.
papers.conclusion: The study reveals multilingual activation patterns in LLMs, their connections to language families and instruction tuning, and provides a new effective approach for model pruning and sparse activation.
papers.key_findings:
Activation patterns differ across languages and correlate with language families and genera.
Multilingual shared experts are concentrated in middle layers, while shallow and deep layers contain more language-specific experts.
Instruction tuning significantly alters activation patterns, with the largest changes in the last layer.
Pruning based on expert activation frequency outperforms random pruning and can exceed the performance of the original unpruned model in some languages.
Different layers exhibit different activation sparsity, so configuring layer-specific pruning rates yields better results.
papers.limitation:
The pruning ratio is limited due to low activation sparsity in most layers of models like Llama 2.
There is a concern that simplified representations may fail to capture the model's out-of-distribution behavior, though evaluation on out-of-distribution tasks provides some mitigation.
future_direction: Extend experiments to a broader array of models and languages.
Explore how to further leverage these insights to utilize and enhance the multilingual capabilities of LLMs.
papers.abstract: Recently, large language models (LLMs) have achieved tremendous breakthroughs in the field of NLP, but still lack understanding of their internal neuron activities when processing different languages. We designed a method to convert dense LLMs into fine-grained MoE architectures, and then visually studied the multilingual activation patterns of LLMs through expert activation frequency heatmaps. Through comprehensive experiments on different model families, different model sizes, and different variants, we analyzed the similarities and differences in the internal neuron activation patterns of LLMs when processing different languages. Specifically, we investigated the distribution of high-frequency activated experts, multilingual shared experts, whether multilingual activation patterns are related to language families, and the impact of instruction tuning on activation patterns. We further explored leveraging the discovered differences in expert activation frequencies to guide sparse activation and pruning. Experimental results demonstrated that our method significantly outperformed random expert pruning and even exceeded the performance of unpruned models in some languages. Additionally, we found that configuring different pruning rates for different layers based on activation level differences could achieve better results. Our findings reveal the multilingual processing mechanisms within LLMs and utilize these insights to offer new perspectives for applications such as sparse activation and model pruning.

papers.title: From Monolingual to Bilingual: Investigating Language Conditioning in Large Language Models for Psycholinguistic Tasks
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode psycholinguistic knowledge across languages, and how does language identity (monolingual vs bilingual prompting) affect their output behavior and internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that large language models condition their psycholinguistic behavior and internal representations on the language identity specified in the prompt, with differences between monolingual and bilingual prompting, offering insights into cross-linguistic cognition in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: Overall, our results demonstrate that LLMs are not language-neutral. Instead, they respond to and encode language-specific cues in both their outputs and internal representations.
papers.key_findings:
Both models adapt their outputs based on the linguistic identity embedded in the prompt.
Qwen shows greater sensitivity to prompt language and sharper behavioral distinctions between Dutch and Chinese than Llama.
Probing reveals that psycholinguistic signals become more linearly decodable in deeper layers.
Chinese prompts yield stronger and more stable valence representations than Dutch prompts.
Bilingual prompting can introduce interference or noise, especially for low-resource languages like Dutch.
papers.limitation:
Focus on only three languages (English, Dutch, Chinese), limiting generalizability.
Only two LLMs are evaluated.
Tasks represent only a narrow slice of the psycholinguistic space.
future_direction: Expanding to include languages with different scripts, phonological systems, or morphological complexity (e.g., Arabic, Hindi, Finnish).
Incorporating a broader set of psycholinguistic phenomena, such as lexical decision making, semantic priming, syntactic ambiguity resolution, and metaphor comprehension.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit strong linguistic capabilities, but little is known about how they encode psycholinguistic knowledge across languages. We investigate whether and how LLMs exhibit human-like psycholinguistic responses under different linguistic identities using two tasks: sound symbolism and word valence. We evaluate two models, Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct, under monolingual and bilingual prompting in English, Dutch, and Chinese. Behaviorally, both models adjust their outputs based on prompted language identity, with Qwen showing greater sensitivity and sharper distinctions between Dutch and Chinese. Probing analysis reveals that psycholinguistic signals become more decodable in deeper layers, with Chinese prompts yielding stronger and more stable valence representations than Dutch. Our results demonstrate that language identity conditions both output behavior and internal representations in LLMs, providing new insights into their application as models of cross-linguistic cognition.

papers.title: Mechanistic Understanding and Mitigation of Language Confusion in English-Centric Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How does language confusion arise mechanistically in English-centric LLMs, and can it be mitigated through neuron-level interventions?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides the first mechanistic interpretability study of language confusion in LLMs, revealing that confusion points arise from transition failures in final layers and can be effectively mitigated by editing a small set of critical neurons identified through comparative analysis.
papers.conclusion: This work provides the first mechanistic interpretability account of language confusion in English-centric LLMs, demonstrating that targeted neuron editing can robustly mitigate confusion without sacrificing general competence or fluency.
papers.key_findings:
Confusion points are critical drivers of language confusion, and token replacement at these points reduces confusion.
Layer-wise analysis shows that language confusion is caused by failed transitions to the target language in the final layers.
Neuron-level analysis identifies specific FFN neurons in late layers that are responsible for confusion points.
Comparative importance selection of neurons enables effective mitigation of language confusion through editing.
Neuron editing achieves confusion reduction comparable to multilingual tuning for many languages while preserving general competence and output quality.
papers.limitation:
Analysis primarily focuses on the monolingual setting; cross-lingual contexts are left for future research.
Neuron editing interventions may require further validation across broader domains and model architectures.
Fully understanding how these mechanisms interact with other multilingual phenomena warrants further investigation.
future_direction: Extending analysis to cross-lingual contexts
Validating neuron editing across broader domains and model architectures
Investigating interactions with other multilingual phenomena
papers.abstract: Language confusion -- where large language models (LLMs) generate unintended languages against the user's need -- remains a critical challenge, especially for English-centric models. We present the first mechanistic interpretability (MI) study of language confusion, combining behavioral benchmarking with neuron-level analysis. Using the Language Confusion Benchmark (LCB), we show that confusion points (CPs) -- specific positions where language switches occur -- are central to this phenomenon. Through layer-wise analysis with TunedLens and targeted neuron attribution, we reveal that transition failures in the final layers drive confusion. We further demonstrate that editing a small set of critical neurons, identified via comparative analysis with a multilingual-tuned counterpart, substantially mitigates confusion while largely preserving general competence and fluency. Our approach matches multilingual alignment in confusion reduction for many languages and yields cleaner, higher-quality outputs. These findings provide new insights into the internal dynamics of LLMs and highlight neuron-level interventions as a promising direction for robust, interpretable multilingual language modeling. Code and data are available at: https://github.com/ercong21/lang_confusion.

papers.title: Understanding the role of FFNs in driving multilingual behaviour in LLMs
papers.research_question: How do Feed-Forward Networks (FFNs) in large language models drive multilingual behavior, and what are the patterns of multilingual processing across layers and model sizes?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the metric 'activation flatness' and analyzes FFN sublayers (detectors and combinators) to reveal distinct patterns of multilingual processing, identifying the phenomenon of 'over-layerization' where increasing layer depth without other adjustments can degrade performance.
papers.conclusion: The analysis reveals distinct patterns in FFN sublayers for multilingual processing, with detectors becoming more peaked and language-specific in later layers, and combinators showing multilingual behavior in middle layers, while also identifying over-layerization in certain model configurations.
papers.key_findings:
FFN representations are more sparse near the input and output layers across all models.
Detector activations become more peaked (less flat) through the layers, while combinator activations show a distinct drop in flatness around layer 20 regardless of model size.
Early detector layers are multilingual and process shallow features, becoming more language-specific near the output.
Combinator layers are mostly multilingual in the middle layers, with the final layers becoming language-specific, especially in larger models.
The 2.9B parameter model exhibits 'over-layerization', where increased layer depth without corresponding adjustments leads to degraded generation quality compared to the 7.5B model.
papers.limitation:
The analysis relies only on model snapshots (activations), which does not fully capture the complexities of LLMs; probing tasks or attention matrices could provide a more comprehensive understanding.
The investigation is limited to the XGLM model family, and findings may not generalize to other LLM architectures or implementations.
The analysis is limited to a set of predefined languages and test sets, which may not fully represent linguistic diversity.
future_direction: Investigate whether flatter activation patterns are easier to adapt in QLoRA fine-tuning.
Extend the analysis to more languages and explore cross-linguistic variation in more detail.
papers.abstract: Multilingualism in Large Language Models (LLMs) is an yet under-explored area. In this paper, we conduct an in-depth analysis of the multilingual capabilities of a family of a Large Language Model, examining its architecture, activation patterns, and processing mechanisms across languages. We introduce novel metrics to probe the model's multilingual behaviour at different layers and shed light on the impact of architectural choices on multilingual processing. Our findings reveal different patterns of multilinugal processing in the sublayers of Feed-Forward Networks of the models. Furthermore, we uncover the phenomenon of "over-layerization" in certain model configurations, where increasing layer depth without corresponding adjustments to other parameters may degrade model performance. Through comparisons within and across languages, we demonstrate the interplay between model architecture, layer depth, and multilingual processing capabilities of LLMs trained on multiple languages.

papers.title: Open Sesame: Getting inside BERT’s Linguistic Knowledge
papers.research_question: How and to what extent does BERT encode syntactically-sensitive hierarchical information or positionally-sensitive linear information?
papers.core_contribution: BERT encodes positional information in lower layers and switches to a hierarchically-oriented encoding on higher layers. The paper also introduces a 'confusion score' to quantify intrusion effects in BERT's self-attention mechanism.
papers.conclusion: BERT composes increasingly abstract hierarchical representations of linguistic structure using self-attention, but does not show the sharp sensitivity to hierarchical structure found in human processing.
papers.key_findings:
Diagnostic classifiers show BERT's lower layers encode positional information well, while higher layers encode hierarchical information.
The proposed confusion score reveals BERT's attention is sensitive to syntactic structure and grammatical features (number, gender) in subject-verb agreement and reflexive anaphora.
BERT's attention is not perfectly syntactic; it sometimes attends to grammatically inaccessible or mismatched distractors.
Confusion scores decrease with layer depth, and there is an increase in confusion at layer 4, coinciding with the degradation of positional information.
BERT's performance on possessive constructions in the subject noun task is poor, possibly due to ambiguity of the 's token.
papers.limitation:
BERT performed poorly on possessive constructions in the subject noun task, possibly due to ambiguity of the 's token.
BERT's attention is only incompletely modulated by structural and featural properties, and attention is sometimes spread across grammatically irrelevant elements.
future_direction: Investigate or visualize layer-on-layer changes in BERT’s structural and positional information, particularly between layers 3 and 4.
Retrieve the increasingly hierarchical representations of BERT across layers via the self-attention mechanism.
papers.abstract: How and to what extent does BERT encode syntactically-sensitive hierarchical information or positionally-sensitive linear information? Recent work has shown that contextual representations like BERT perform well on tasks that require sensitivity to linguistic structure. We present here two studies which aim to provide a better understanding of the nature of BERT's representations. The first of these focuses on the identification of structurally-defined elements using diagnostic classifiers, while the second explores BERT's representation of subject-verb agreement and anaphor-antecedent dependencies through a quantitative assessment of self-attention vectors. In both cases, we find that BERT encodes positional information about word tokens well on its lower layers, but switches to a hierarchically-oriented encoding on higher layers. We conclude then that BERT's representations do indeed model linguistically relevant aspects of hierarchical structure, though they do not appear to show the sharp sensitivity to hierarchical structure that is found in human processing of reflexive anaphora.

papers.title: Identifying and Controlling Important Neurons in Neural Machine\n Translation
papers.research_question: How important are individual neurons for obtaining high-quality translations? Do individual neurons in NMT models contain interpretable linguistic information? Can we control MT output by intervening in the representation at the individual neuron level?
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops unsupervised methods (based on correlations between models) for discovering important neurons in Neural Machine Translation models, shows these neurons impact translation quality and capture linguistic phenomena, and demonstrates how to control translations by modifying their activations.
papers.conclusion: The work indicates that not all information is distributed in NMT models, and that many human-interpretable grammatical and structural properties are captured by individual neurons. Moreover, modifying the activations of individual neurons allows controlling the translation output according to specified linguistic properties.
papers.key_findings:
Unsupervised correlation methods (MaxCorr, MinCorr, LinReg, SVCCA) can rank neurons by importance, with top-ranked neurons having a larger impact on translation quality when erased.
Many top-ranked neurons capture interpretable linguistic properties such as position in sentence, parentheses, tense, number, gender, and noun phrase segmentation.
Modifying the activations of individual neurons (e.g., tense neurons) allows for controlling translation output (e.g., changing verb tense) with varying degrees of success.
Different ranking methods highlight different types of information: MaxCorr and MinCorr tend to find position information, while LinReg and SVCCA find information distributed across tokens.
The work indicates that not all linguistic information in NMT models is fully distributed; some properties are captured by individual neurons.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to other NMT components (e.g., the decoder) and architectures (e.g., Transformer, convolutional seq2seq).
Develop more sophisticated ways to control translation output, for example by modifying representations in variational NMT architectures.
Apply the methods to other tasks beyond machine translation.
papers.abstract:
Neural machine translation (NMT) models learn representations containing
substantial linguistic information. However, it is not clear if such
information is fully distributed or if some of it can be attributed to
individual neurons. We develop unsupervised methods for discovering important
neurons in NMT models. Our methods rely on the intuition that different models
learn similar properties, and do not require any costly external supervision.
We show experimentally that translation quality depends on the discovered
neurons, and find that many of them capture common linguistic phenomena.
Finally, we show how to control NMT translations in predictable ways, by
modifying activations of individual neurons.

papers.title: Focusing on Language: Revealing and Exploiting Language Attention Heads in Multilingual Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the role of multi-head self-attention in supporting multilingual processing in LLMs? Specifically, are there language-specific and language-general attention heads, and how can they be used to control model behavior?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces LAHIS, a method to identify language-specific and language-general attention heads in multilingual LLMs, and shows how modulating these heads can control cross-lingual attention and improve multilingual performance with minimal parameters.
papers.conclusion: The work enhances interpretability of multilingual behaviors in LLMs from the perspective of MHA and presents practical approaches to strengthen multilingual capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
LAHIS reveals the existence of language-specific and language-general attention heads in multilingual LLMs.
Language-specific heads enable cross-lingual attention transfer, allowing steering of model attention to target languages.
Modulating language-specific heads mitigates off-target language generation by suppressing English-heads.
A lightweight adaptation using a trainable matrix on language-specific heads improves multilingual question answering accuracy with only 14-20 parameters.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly support multilingual understanding and generation. Meanwhile, efforts to interpret their internal mechanisms have emerged, offering insights to enhance multilingual performance. While multi-head self-attention (MHA) has proven critical in many areas, its role in multilingual capabilities remains underexplored. In this work, we study the contribution of MHA in supporting multilingual processing in LLMs. We propose Language Attention Head Importance Scores (LAHIS), an effective and efficient method that identifies attention head importance for multilingual capabilities via a single forward and backward pass through the LLM. Applying LAHIS to Aya-23-8B, Llama-3.2-3B, and Mistral-7B-v0.1, we reveal the existence of both language-specific and language-general heads. Language-specific heads enable cross-lingual attention transfer to guide the model toward target language contexts and mitigate off-target language generation issue, contributing to addressing challenges in multilingual LLMs. We also introduce a lightweight adaptation that learns a soft head mask to modulate attention outputs over language heads, requiring only 20 tunable parameters to improve XQuAD accuracy. Overall, our work enhances both the interpretability and multilingual capabilities of LLMs from the perspective of MHA.

papers.title: Unveiling Linguistic Regions in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether a core linguistic region exists within LLMs that facilitates cross-lingual alignment and generalization, whether distinct monolingual regions exist for individual languages, and how these regions affect further pre-training and can be used to mitigate catastrophic forgetting.
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers that LLMs possess a core linguistic region (about 1% of parameters) whose removal causes a complete loss of linguistic competence, and distinct monolingual regions for individual languages. It also shows that freezing the core region during further pre-training mitigates catastrophic forgetting.
papers.conclusion: The paper identifies a core region essential for multilingual alignment and generalization in LLMs, whose removal causes complete linguistic competence loss. Freezing this region during further pre-training alleviates catastrophic forgetting, providing new perspectives on LLMs' linguistic competence.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs possess a core linguistic region, and removing this region (setting parameters to zero) results in a significant loss of the model's linguistic capabilities across 30 languages.
This core region exhibits significant dimensional dependence; perturbations to specific dimensions or even a single parameter can lead to a substantial decline in linguistic ability.
Distinct monolingual regions exist in LLMs for different languages. Removing a specific monolingual region causes a significant deterioration in the linguistic capabilities within the corresponding language.
Freezing the core linguistic region during further pre-training can mitigate the issue of catastrophic forgetting, a common phenomenon observed during further pre-training of LLMs.
The core linguistic region is concentrated in specific rows and columns of the attention and feedforward layer matrices, and its removal leads to a complete loss of model proficiency.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are based on LLaMA-2-7B/13B, and it remains to be further determined whether the same phenomena are observable in larger or differently architected models.
Optimizing full-scale fine-tuning through the freezing operation is not suited to extensive datasets. A more feasible approach is to limit the magnitude of parameter updates.
future_direction: Exploring whether the same phenomena are observable in larger or differently architected models.
Using a more feasible approach of limiting the magnitude of parameter updates instead of freezing for extensive datasets.
Exploring knowledge as a higher-level semantic representation beyond language.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated considerable cross-lingual alignment and generalization ability. Current research primarily focuses on improving LLMs' cross-lingual generalization capabilities. However, there is still a lack of research on the intrinsic mechanisms of how LLMs achieve cross-lingual alignment. From the perspective of region partitioning, this paper conducts several investigations on the linguistic competence of LLMs. We discover a core region in LLMs that corresponds to linguistic competence, accounting for approximately 1% of the total model parameters. Removing this core region by setting parameters to zero results in a significant performance decrease across 30 different languages. Furthermore, this core region exhibits significant dimensional dependence, perturbations to even a single parameter on specific dimensions leading to a loss of linguistic competence. Moreover, we discover that distinct monolingual regions exist for different languages, and disruption to these specific regions substantially reduces the LLMs' proficiency in those corresponding languages. Our research also indicates that freezing the core linguistic region during further pre-training can mitigate the issue of catastrophic forgetting (CF), a common phenomenon observed during further pre-training of LLMs. Overall, exploring the LLMs' functional regions provides insights into the foundation of their intelligence.

papers.title: How a Bilingual LM Becomes Bilingual: Tracing Internal Representations with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How do bilingual language models develop internal representations, specifically when, where, and how does bilingual alignment emerge during pre-training?
papers.core_contribution: Bilingual language models first learn languages separately and then gradually form bilingual alignments, particularly in mid-layers, with larger models showing stronger alignment; bilingual representations are critical for performance, as shown by an intervention method that injects bilingual features from a fully trained model into a mid-training model.
papers.conclusion: Bilingual language models initially learn languages independently and later develop bilingual alignments, especially in mid-layers of larger models, and sparse autoencoders can be used for both analysis and intervention.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs initially learn languages independently and gradually develop bilingual alignment over training.
Bilingual alignments are more prominently captured in the mid-layers of the model.
Larger models exhibit stronger bilingual alignment than smaller ones.
Bilingual representations from a fully trained model enhance the performance of a mid-training model when injected.
The model's internal representations evolve from language-specific to bilingual semantic alignment as training progresses.
papers.limitation:
The study focuses on English and Japanese, so findings may not generalize to all language pairs.
The interpretability of sparse autoencoders is limited and reconstruction accuracy is not perfect, so analysis is based on an approximation.
future_direction: Investigate a wider range of language pairs to validate and extend the observations.
Combine sparse autoencoders with other analytical methods for a more robust understanding.
papers.abstract: This study explores how bilingual language models develop complex internal representations. We employ sparse autoencoders to analyze internal representations of bilingual language models with a focus on the effects of training steps, layers, and model sizes. Our analysis shows that language models first learn languages separately, and then gradually form bilingual alignments, particularly in the mid layers. We also found that this bilingual tendency is stronger in larger models. Building on these findings, we demonstrate the critical role of bilingual representations in model performance by employing a novel method that integrates decomposed representations from a fully trained model into a mid-training model. Our results provide insights into how language models acquire bilingual capabilities.

papers.title: Contextual Gradient Interference: A Novel Mechanism for Knowledge Retention and Adaptability in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How to mitigate catastrophic forgetting in large language models by enabling knowledge retention while adapting to new tasks through a gradient-based mechanism?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Contextual Gradient Interference mechanism, a dual-gradient framework that dynamically partitions parameter updates to mitigate catastrophic forgetting and enhance knowledge retention and adaptability in large language models.
papers.conclusion: The Contextual Gradient Interference mechanism successfully addresses catastrophic forgetting by balancing knowledge preservation and task adaptation, demonstrating improved performance and scalability in large language models.
papers.key_findings:
The CGI mechanism improves accuracy, reduces perplexity, and enhances retention scores across various tasks.
It outperforms baseline models in retention scores for sequential learning tasks.
The model shows adaptability to variable contexts, though performance declines with increased complexity in multi-hop reasoning.
Scalability tests show accuracy plateaus beyond 100GB dataset size, with training time increasing non-linearly.
The model is robust to noisy inputs but accuracy decreases with higher noise levels.
papers.limitation:
Increased computational overhead associated with gradient decomposition and real-time masking
Reliance on auxiliary loss functions requiring careful hyperparameter calibration
Sensitivity to input quality under noisy conditions
future_direction: Investigating alternative methods for gradient decomposition, such as sparse or low-rank approximations
Incorporating reinforcement learning paradigms to dynamically adjust masking parameters based on task feedback
Exploring integration with emerging architectures, such as sparse attention or memory-augmented transformers
papers.abstract: Addressing the challenge of catastrophic forgetting in large-scale neural architectures requires innovative solutions that enable models to retain prior knowledge while adapting to new tasks. The proposed Contextual Gradient Interference mechanism introduces a dual-gradient framework designed to partition parameter updates dynamically, ensuring stability for previously learned information while facilitating effective task-specific adaptations. By leveraging real-time gradient analysis and masking strategies, the mechanism mitigates interference and promotes efficient learning across sequential tasks. The integration of this approach within the Falcon model, a state-of-the-art open-source language model, demonstrated significant improvements in knowledge retention, task adaptability, and robustness under varying conditions, including noisy inputs and increasing dataset sizes. Quantitative evaluations across multiple benchmarks revealed enhanced accuracy, lower perplexity, and improved memory retention compared to existing methodologies. The scalability of the approach was further validated through its computational efficiency and performance consistency over extended training cycles. Additional experiments highlighted the ability of the model to handle multi-hop reasoning and sequential tasks with complex contextual dependencies, showcasing the versatility of the proposed mechanism. An ablation study reinforced the significance of key components, such as gradient masking and decomposition, in achieving the observed performance gains. Results also revealed areas for potential optimization, including computational trade-offs and sensitivity to hyperparameter configurations. The study advances the understanding of gradient-based learning strategies and their critical role in optimizing neural networks for dynamic and large-scale tasks. Through its novel contributions, the mechanism establishes a foundation for enhancing the stability, adaptability, and efficiency of language model training, making it an invaluable tool for future developments in machine learning.

papers.title: Revisiting Modality Invariance in a Multilingual Speech-Text Model via Neuron-Level Analysis
papers.research_question: How and when do multilingual speech–text models reuse shared circuitry across modalities, and how does this reuse differ between input-language representation and output-language generation during decoding?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a generation-step-aware framework for cross-modal evaluation of multilingual speech-text models, revealing that cross-modal language alignment is time- and function-dependent, with representation alignment strongest at early steps and control alignment strengthening later.
papers.conclusion: Cross-modal processing in multilingual speech-text models is both time-dependent and function-dependent, highlighting the importance of generation-aware diagnostics for evaluating multilingual behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Cross-modal language alignment for language-representation neurons is strongest at the first decoding step but weakens as generation proceeds, indicating a shift from shared to modality-specific processing.
Language-control neurons identified from speech transfer causally to text generation, revealing partially shared circuitry for output-language control.
The cross-modal effect ratio for language control increases at later decoding steps, showing stronger transfer of control mechanisms.
The distribution of language-selective neurons shifts from self-attention to cross-attention as decoding proceeds, indicating a transition from encoder-driven to autoregressive processing.
Cross-modal neuron overlap shows a strong diagonal (same-language) preference at the first step, which weakens at later steps.
papers.limitation:
Focus on a single model architecture (SeamlessM4T v2).
Reliance on AP-based neuron identification, which captures statistical associations but does not establish causal necessity.
Use of synthetic speech to control for acoustic variability, which may not fully reflect natural speech.
Asymmetries across tasks (e.g., ASR vs. text repetition) and language tags might introduce noise in neuron identification and cross-modal comparisons.
future_direction: Verify whether similar patterns hold for natural speech.
Explore more symmetric settings, such as En→X translation across modalities.
papers.abstract: Multilingual speech-text foundation models aim to process language uniformly across both modality and language, yet it remains unclear whether they internally represent the same language consistently when it is spoken versus written. We investigate this question in SeamlessM4T v2 through three complementary analyses that probe where language and modality information is encoded, how selective neurons causally influence decoding, and how concentrated this influence is across the network. We identify language- and modality-selective neurons using average-precision ranking, investigate their functional role via median-replacement interventions at inference time, and analyze activation-magnitude inequality across languages and modalities. Across experiments, we find evidence of incomplete modality invariance. Although encoder representations become increasingly language-agnostic, this compression makes it more difficult for the shared decoder to recover the language of origin when constructing modality-agnostic representations, particularly when adapting from speech to text. We further observe sharply localized modality-selective structure in cross-attention key and value projections. Finally, speech-conditioned decoding and non-dominant scripts exhibit higher activation concentration, indicating heavier reliance on a small subset of neurons, which may underlie increased brittleness across modalities and languages.

papers.title: The Geometry of Multilingual Language Model Representations
papers.research_question: How do multilingual language models maintain a shared multilingual representation space while still encoding language-sensitive information in each language?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that multilingual language models encode information along orthogonal language-sensitive and language-neutral axes, facilitating feature extraction for downstream tasks and cross-lingual transfer learning.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual language models encode features along orthogonal language-sensitive and language-neutral axes, enabling targeted extraction of features for downstream tasks and cross-lingual transfer learning.
papers.key_findings:
Languages occupy similar linear subspaces after mean-centering, as shown by causal effects on language modeling performance and direct subspace comparisons.
Subspace means differ along language-sensitive axes that encode information such as token vocabularies, and shifting representations by language means is sufficient to induce token predictions in different languages.
Stable language-neutral axes encode information such as token positions and part-of-speech, and these axes are orthogonal to language-sensitive axes.
The identified axes (both language-sensitive and language-neutral) are relatively stable across middle layers of the model.
Token position information is encoded along nonlinear structures like spirals, toruses, and curves in the representation space.
future_direction: Investigate how nonlinear structures (e.g., spirals, toruses) arise from and interact with the dot product self-attention mechanism in Transformer models.
Conduct a more detailed analysis of how specific representational structures are retained across layers.

Assess how multilingual language models encode more complex linguistic features geometrically, and the extent to which representation spaces can be fully decomposed into orthogonal subspaces encoding different features.
papers.abstract: We assess how multilingual language models maintain a shared multilingual representation space while still encoding language-sensitive information in each language. Using XLM-R as a case study, we show that languages occupy similar linear subspaces after mean-centering, evaluated based on causal effects on language modeling performance and direct comparisons between subspaces for 88 languages. The subspace means differ along language-sensitive axes that are relatively stable throughout middle layers, and these axes encode information such as token vocabularies. Shifting representations by language means is sufficient to induce token predictions in different languages. However, we also identify stable language-neutral axes that encode information such as token positions and part-of-speech. We visualize representations projected onto language-sensitive and language-neutral axes, identifying language family and part-of-speech clusters, along with spirals, toruses, and curves representing token position information. These results demonstrate that multilingual language models encode information along orthogonal language-sensitive and language-neutral axes, allowing the models to extract a variety of features for downstream tasks and cross-lingual transfer learning.

papers.title: Language Models Represent Space and Time
papers.research_question: Do large language models learn coherent linear representations of space and time, i.e., do they form a world model?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models learn linear representations of space and time that are robust to prompting and unified across entity types, and individual 'space' and 'time' neurons exist that encode these coordinates.
papers.conclusion: Modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes can recover spatial and temporal coordinates from internal activations, with performance increasing with model size and plateauing in middle layers.
Spatial and temporal features are linearly represented, as nonlinear probes do not improve performance.
Representations are robust to variations in prompting, though random tokens or capitalization degrade performance.
Probes generalize across entity types and to held-out geographic or temporal blocks, indicating unified representations.
Individual neurons exist that are highly predictive of space and time, and causal interventions confirm their importance.
papers.limitation:
Data comes only from English Wikipedia, skewing towards the Anglosphere, and entity type distribution is not uniform.
The true extent and structure of spatial and temporal representations remain unclear.
future_direction: Extracting representations in the model’s coordinate system rather than human coordinates, e.g., with sparse autoencoders.
Studying how these spatiotemporal representations are learned, recalled, and used internally across training checkpoints.
Investigating potential parallels with biological place and grid cells in the brain.
papers.abstract: The capabilities of large language models (LLMs) have sparked debate over whether such systems just learn an enormous collection of superficial statistics or a set of more coherent and grounded representations that reflect the real world. We find evidence for the latter by analyzing the learned representations of three spatial datasets (world, US, NYC places) and three temporal datasets (historical figures, artworks, news headlines) in the Llama-2 family of models. We discover that LLMs learn linear representations of space and time across multiple scales. These representations are robust to prompting variations and unified across different entity types (e.g. cities and landmarks). In addition, we identify individual "space neurons" and "time neurons" that reliably encode spatial and temporal coordinates. While further investigation is needed, our results suggest modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.

papers.title: Mechanistic Analysis of Catastrophic Forgetting in Large Language Models During Continual Fine-tuning
papers.research_question: What are the primary mechanisms driving catastrophic forgetting in large language models during continual fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies three primary mechanisms of catastrophic forgetting in LLMs during sequential fine-tuning: gradient interference in attention weights, representational drift in intermediate layers, and loss landscape flattening around prior task minima.
papers.conclusion: Catastrophic forgetting in LLMs is driven by three interacting mechanisms (attention disruption, representational drift, loss landscape flattening), providing a mechanistic foundation for developing targeted continual learning strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Approximately 15-23% of attention heads, particularly in lower layers, undergo severe disruption during fine-tuning, driving early forgetting.
Representational drift in intermediate layers, measured by CKA similarity, decreases by 0.32 to 0.47, indicating significant geometric changes.
Gradient interference, especially in query and key projection matrices, strongly predicts forgetting severity (correlation r=0.87).
The loss landscape around previous task minima flattens substantially (maximum Hessian eigenvalue drops from 147.3 to 34.2), making recovery difficult.
These three mechanisms interact and operate at different timescales, with attention disruption early, representational drift accumulating, and landscape flattening emerging later.
papers.limitation:
Experimental design focused on task sequences with clear boundaries, not continuous adaptation to gradually shifting distributions.
Examined forgetting over relatively short task sequences (4 to 6 tasks), while practical systems may encounter hundreds of sequential tasks.
Mechanistic analysis primarily characterized average behaviors across many model instances; understanding individual variability and rare failure modes remains important.
future_direction: Developing architecture modifications that inherently resist the identified forgetting mechanisms, such as attention heads with built-in stability constraints or intermediate layers with protected representational subspaces.
Designing optimization algorithms that explicitly manage gradient interference, representational drift, and landscape geometry during fine-tuning.
Creating diagnostic tools that monitor mechanistic signatures in real-time to prevent catastrophic forgetting before it occurs.
papers.abstract: Large language models exhibit remarkable performance across diverse tasks through pre-training and fine-tuning paradigms. However, continual fine-tuning on sequential tasks induces catastrophic forgetting, where newly acquired knowledge interferes with previously learned capabilities. Despite widespread observations of this phenomenon, the mechanistic understanding remains limited. Here, we present a comprehensive mechanistic analysis of catastrophic forgetting in transformer-based LLMs during sequential fine-tuning. Through systematic experiments across multiple model scales (109B to 400B total parameters) and task sequences, we identify three primary mechanisms driving forgetting: gradient interference in attention weights, representational drift in intermediate layers, and loss landscape flattening. We demonstrate that forgetting severity correlates strongly with task similarity (Pearson r = 0.87) and gradient alignment metrics. Our analysis reveals that approximately 15 to 23 percent of attention heads undergo severe disruption during fine-tuning, with lower layers showing greater susceptibility. These findings establish mechanistic foundations for developing targeted mitigation strategies in continual learning systems.

papers.title: How Do Vision Transformers Work?
papers.research_question: How do multi-head self-attentions (MSAs) and Vision Transformers (ViTs) work? Specifically, what properties of MSAs improve optimization, how do MSAs differ from convolutional layers (Convs), and how can we harmonize MSAs with Convs?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that MSAs in Vision Transformers act as generalized spatial smoothing, flattening loss landscapes and improving generalization, and are complementary to convolutional layers as low-pass vs. high-pass filters. Based on these insights, the paper proposes AlterNet, a model that alternates Conv and MSA blocks, which outperforms CNNs even on small datasets.
papers.conclusion: MSAs are generalized spatial smoothings that complement Convs, and harmonizing them via an alternating pattern leads to models that outperform CNNs across data regimes.
papers.key_findings:
MSAs improve accuracy and generalization by flattening loss landscapes, primarily due to data specificity rather than long-range dependency.
MSAs are low-pass filters that reduce high-frequency signals and aggregate feature maps, while Convs are high-pass filters that amplify high-frequency signals and diversify feature maps.
ViTs suffer from non-convex losses in small data regimes, which can be alleviated by large datasets or loss landscape smoothing methods.
Multi-stage neural networks behave like series connections of small individual models, and MSAs at the end of a stage play a key role in prediction.
The proposed AlterNet, which alternates Conv and MSA blocks, outperforms CNNs not only on large datasets but also on small datasets.
papers.limitation: The effects of data augmentation on loss landscapes and uncertainty calibration require further investigation.
future_direction: Further investigation into the effects of data augmentation on uncertainty calibration and loss landscapes.
papers.abstract: The success of multi-head self-attentions (MSAs) for computer vision is now indisputable. However, little is known about how MSAs work. We present fundamental explanations to help better understand the nature of MSAs. In particular, we demonstrate the following properties of MSAs and Vision Transformers (ViTs): (1) MSAs improve not only accuracy but also generalization by flattening the loss landscapes. Such improvement is primarily attributable to their data specificity, not long-range dependency. On the other hand, ViTs suffer from non-convex losses. Large datasets and loss landscape smoothing methods alleviate this problem; (2) MSAs and Convs exhibit opposite behaviors. For example, MSAs are low-pass filters, but Convs are high-pass filters. Therefore, MSAs and Convs are complementary; (3) Multi-stage neural networks behave like a series connection of small individual models. In addition, MSAs at the end of a stage play a key role in prediction. Based on these insights, we propose AlterNet, a model in which Conv blocks at the end of a stage are replaced with MSA blocks. AlterNet outperforms CNNs not only in large data regimes but also in small data regimes. The code is available at https://github.com/xxxnell/how-do-vits-work.

papers.title: Can Transformer be Too Compositional? Analysing Idiom Processing in Neural Machine Translation
papers.research_question: How does the Transformer-based neural machine translation model process idioms, and is the non-compositionality of idioms reflected in its mechanics?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer tends to translate idioms too compositionally, and when it produces non-literal translations, the encoder groups idiom parts more strongly as a single unit, with reduced interaction with context and reduced cross-attention on source tokens.
papers.conclusion: Transformer's tendency to process idioms compositionally contributes to literal translations, and techniques that encourage compositionality in NMT may be detrimental for non-compositional phenomena like idioms.
papers.key_findings:
Figurative idioms receive more attention within the PIE in encoder self-attention compared to literal idioms.
Figurative idioms have reduced attention between the PIE and its context.
In cross-attention, figurative idioms lead to reduced attention on source-side PIE tokens and increased attention on the </s> token.
Hidden representations of figurative idioms change more across layers than those of literal idioms.
Intervening with INLP to remove linearly encoded features of figurativeness can change paraphrased translations to word-for-word, indicating a causal link.
papers.limitation:
Heuristic annotation method for translations has imperfect accuracy (75-89% for key categories).
Analysis is limited to seven European languages.
future_direction: Architectural changes to improve grouping of idioms as single units, e.g., training specific attention heads or penalizing overly compositional translations.
Evaluate the effect of compositionality-favouring techniques on non-compositional phenomena like idioms.
papers.abstract: Unlike literal expressions, idioms' meanings do not directly follow from their parts, posing a challenge for neural machine translation (NMT). NMT models are often unable to translate idioms accurately and over-generate compositional, literal translations. In this work, we investigate whether the non-compositionality of idioms is reflected in the mechanics of the dominant NMT model, Transformer, by analysing the hidden states and attention patterns for models with English as source language and one of seven European languages as target language.When Transformer emits a non-literal translation - i.e. identifies the expression as idiomatic - the encoder processes idioms more strongly as single lexical units compared to literal expressions. This manifests in idioms' parts being grouped through attention and in reduced interaction between idioms and their context.In the decoder's cross-attention, figurative inputs result in reduced attention on source-side tokens. These results suggest that Transformer's tendency to process idioms as compositional expressions contributes to literal translations of idioms.

papers.title: High-Dimensional Interlingual Representations of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do multilingual large language models develop a universal interlingua representation, or present a partially aligned construct toward certain languages?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework and the Interlingual Local Overlap (ILO) metric to analyze interlingual representations in multilingual LLMs, and shows that selectively freezing early layers during single-language fine-tuning preserves interlingual alignment and improves cross-lingual generalization.
papers.conclusion: Interlingual semantic alignment is crucial for scalable multilingual learning, and the proposed framework and ILO metric provide effective tools for evaluating and preserving this alignment in multilingual LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Multilingual LLMs exhibit inconsistent cross-lingual alignments, with stronger alignment between high-resource languages and within the same linguistic family or region.
Single-language fine-tuning disrupts interlingual alignment, particularly in early layers, leading to degraded cross-lingual generalization.
Selectively freezing early layers (and other alignment-critical parameters) during single-language fine-tuning preserves interlingual alignment and significantly improves cross-lingual transfer performance.
The proposed ILO score effectively quantifies the degree of interlingual alignment by measuring the local neighborhood structure of high-dimensional representations.
Interlingual overlaps that transcend familial and regional boundaries are observed in intermediate model layers, while early and late layers show clustering by resource level and linguistic features.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) trained on massive multilingual datasets hint at the formation of interlingual constructs--a shared subspace in the representation space. However, evidence regarding this phenomenon is mixed, leaving it unclear whether these models truly develop unified interlingual representations, or present a partially aligned constructs. We explore 31 diverse languages varying on their resource-levels, typologies, and geographical regions; and find that multilingual LLMs exhibit inconsistent cross-lingual alignments. To address this, we propose an interlingual representation framework identifying both the shared interlingual semantic subspace and fragmented components, existed due to representational limitations. We introduce Interlingual Local Overlap (ILO) score to quantify interlingual alignment by comparing the local neighborhood structures of high-dimensional representations. We utilize ILO to investigate the impact of single-language fine-tuning on the interlingual representations in multilingual LLMs. Our results indicate that training exclusively on a single language disrupts the alignment in early layers, while freezing these layers preserves the alignment of interlingual representations, leading to improved cross-lingual generalization. These results validate our framework and metric for evaluating interlingual representation, and further underscore that interlingual alignment is crucial for scalable multilingual learning.

papers.title: On Identifiability in Transformers
papers.research_question: What is the identifiability of attention weights and token embeddings in Transformers, and how does context aggregate into hidden tokens?
papers.core_contribution: Attention weights are not identifiable and thus not directly interpretable; effective attention and hidden token attribution are proposed as tools to better understand transformers.
papers.conclusion: Attention distributions are not directly interpretable due to non-identifiability; effective attention and hidden token attribution are useful tools for understanding transformers, and the relationship between token mixing and identifiability warrants further investigation.
papers.key_findings:
Attention weights are not identifiable for sequences longer than the attention head dimension, meaning there are infinitely many attention weights yielding the same output.
Effective attention, which removes the null space component, can diverge from raw attention and provide more reliable explanations.
Contextual word embeddings retain their identity (input token) to a large degree across layers, with identity information encoded in the angle.
Input tokens mix strongly in hidden embeddings, with the contribution of the original token decreasing monotonically with depth but remaining the largest individual contributor in most cases.
Context aggregated into hidden embeddings is mostly local, with long-range dependencies increasing in later layers.
papers.limitation:
Effective attention is not guaranteed to be a probability distribution and may have negative weights.
The relationship between token mixing and identifiability warrants further investigation.
future_direction: Further research to understand effective attention and its variants.
Applying the concepts to compare different transformer variants.
papers.abstract: In this paper we delve deep in the Transformer architecture by investigating two of its core components: self-attention and contextual embeddings. In particular, we study the identifiability of attention weights and token embeddings, and the aggregation of context into hidden tokens. We show that, for sequences longer than the attention head dimension, attention weights are not identifiable. We propose effective attention as a complementary tool for improving explanatory interpretations based on attention. Furthermore, we show that input tokens retain to a large degree their identity across the model. We also find evidence suggesting that identity information is mainly encoded in the angle of the embeddings and gradually decreases with depth. Finally, we demonstrate strong mixing of input information in the generation of contextual embeddings by means of a novel quantification method based on gradient attribution. Overall, we show that self-attention distributions are not directly interpretable and present tools to better understand and further investigate Transformer models.

papers.title: exBERT: A Visual Analysis Tool to Explore Learned Representations in Transformer Models
papers.research_question: How can we develop an interactive tool to explore learned representations and attentions in Transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces EXBERT, an interactive visualization tool for exploring learned representations and attentions in Transformer models, enabling hypothesis formulation and replication of prior analyses.
papers.conclusion: EXBERT is a tool that provides interactive insights into Transformer models' representations and attentions, facilitating hypothesis generation and analysis.
papers.key_findings:
